    4. Classes, Records, Interfaces

    4.1. Objects by Example

    4.1.1. Overview

    We will now explore object-oriented programming through examples. An object is an entity that contains data defining its state (referred to as fields, attributes, etc.) and functions (referred to as methods). An object is created based on a template called a class. For example, a class named [C1] declares two fields, [Type1 p1;] and [Type2 p2;], and two methods, [Type3 m3(...) { ... }] and [Type4 m4(...) { ... }], all enclosed within the curly braces of the declaration [public class C1 { ... }].

    From the class [C1], you can create many objects such as [o1], [o2], … All of them will have the fields [p1], [p2], … and the methods [m3], [m4], … However, they will have different values for their [pi] fields, thus each having its own unique state. If [o1] is an object of type [C1], [o1.p1] refers to the [p1] field of [o1], and [o1.m3(...)] refers to thecall to the [m3] method of [o1].

    Let’s consider an initial object model: the class [Personne].

    4.1.2. A program consisting of multiple files

    In the examples from the previous chapter, a program fit into a single source file. From now on, a program can consist of multiple source files: one class per file, plus the main program. In Java, a public class must be placed in a file that bears its name: the public class [Personne] is in the file [Personne.java]. We store the files for a single program in a folder—in this case, the [Personnes] folder within the [04-classes] folder:

    1
2
3
    Personnes/
  Personne.java     la classe Personne
  Main.java         le programme principal

    Starting with Java 22, the source code launcher—which we already used in the previous chapter—can run a program consisting of multiple files: the command [java Main.java], entered in the [Personnes] folder, compiles the file [Main.java] in memory, then, on demand, the other files in the folder that it needs—in this case, [Personne.java]—and runs the program. No compiled files are written to disk. You can also explicitly compile the files using the [javac] compiler, which writes a [.class] file (intermediate code, or “bytecode”) per class, and then run the program with the command [java], specifying where to find the compiled classes (option [-cp], the “classpath”):

    1
2
3
4
5
6
    > javac -d classes *.java
> ls classes
Main.class
Personne.class
> java -cp classes Main
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

    The multi-file launcher is sufficient for the programs in this chapter, which use only the classes from JDK. When a program requires external libraries, we will use a Maven project, as introduced in Chapter 2: Maven downloads the libraries, compiles the project, and runs it. The files in this chapter can be opened as-is in IntelliJ, IDEA, or VS Code.

    4.1.3. Definition of the Person Class

    The definition of the [Personne] class in the source file [Personne.java] will be as follows:

     1

    public class Personne {
     // attributes (fields)
    private String prenom = "";
    private String nom = "";
    private int age;

     // method
    public void initialise(String p, String n, int age) {
        this.prenom = p;
        this.nom = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

     // method
    public void identifie() {
        IO.println("[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}
    • Line 1: The class is public ([public]): it can be used by all other classes. It does not belong to any package—or, more precisely, it belongs to the unnamed package; packages are discussed at the end of the chapter;
    • Lines 3–5: The three fields of the class. Both strings are initialized with the empty string: otherwise, they would be set to [null] when the object is created (an uninitialized object field is set to [null], a numeric field to 0, and a Boolean field to [false]);
    • lines 8–12: a method that sets the object’s state;
    • lines 15–17: a method that displays the object’s state. [IO] is the Java 25 console I/O class we used in the previous chapter.

    Here we have the definition of a class—that is, a data type. When we create variables of this type, we call them objects or class instances. A class is therefore a template from which objects are constructed. By convention, a class name begins with a capital letter ([Personne]), while a field or method name begins with a lowercase letter ([prenom], [initialise]).

    The members of a class can be data (fields) or methods (functions). These members can be accompanied by one of the following keywords:

    Keyword
    Access
    [private]
    A private member is accessible only by the class’s internal methods
    (none)
    If no keyword is specified, the member is accessible by any method in a class from the same package. This is the default access, known as “package access”
    [protected]
    A protected member is accessible by methods of classes in the same package and by methods of derived classes (see the concept of inheritance below)
    [public]
    A public member is accessible by any method, whether or not it is defined within the class

    In general, a class’s data is declared private, while its methods are declared public. This means that the user of an object (the programmer):

    • will not have direct access to the object’s private data;
    • can call the object’s public methods, including those that provide access to its private data.

    The order in which the members [private], [protected], and [public] are declared is arbitrary. Note that the default access is not private: a field declared without a keyword is visible to all classes in the package. Therefore, you must remember to write [private].

    4.1.4. The method initializes

    What is the role of the method [initialise]? Because [nom], [prenom], and [age] are private members of the [Personne] class, a statement such as [p1.prenom = "Jean";], written in the main program, is invalid. The compiler rejects it:

    1
2
3
4
5
6
    > java Main.java
Main.java:4: error: prenom has private access in Personne
    p1.prenom = "Jean";
      ^
1 error
error: compilation failed

    The compiler message is in English: JDK has no French translation for its messages. It specifies the file and line number of the error, then marks it with a circumflex accent. We need to initialize an object of type [Personne] via a public method. This is the role of the [initialise] method. We will write [p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);]. This syntax is valid because [initialise] is publicly accessible.

    4.1.5. The new operator

    However, something is still missing. The declaration [Personne p1;] declares [p1] as a reference to an object of type *[Personne]*. This object does not yet exist, and therefore [p1] is not initialized. When we then write [p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);], we call the method [initialise] of the object referenced by [p1]. However, this object does not exist, and the compiler reports the error: the local variable [p1] has not been assigned a value.

    1
2
3
4
5
6
    > java Main.java
Main.java:4: error: variable p1 might not have been initialized
    p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    ^
1 error
error: compilation failed

    If we write [Personne p1 = null;] followed by [p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);], we explicitly indicate with the keyword [null] that the variable [p1] does not yet reference any object. The compiler accepts the program, but at runtime, the method call triggers a [NullPointerException] exception:

    1
2
3
    > java Main.java
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "Personne.initialise(String, String, int)" because "<local1>" is null
    at Main.main(Main.java:4)

    Starting with Java 14, the exception message specifies which operation failed; [<local1>] refers to the local variable [p1], whose name was not preserved by the in-memory compilation. For [p1] to reference an object, you must write [Personne p1 = new Personne();].

    This creates an object of type [Personne] that has not yet been initialized: its fields have their default values—in this case, the empty string for [nom] and [prenom], and 0 for [age]. Now that [p1] references an object, the initialization statement for this object, [p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);], is valid.

    4.1.6. The this keyword

    Let’s look at the code for the [initialise] method:

     8
 9
10
11
12
        public void initialise(String p, String n, int age) {
        this.prenom = p;
        this.nom = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

    The statement [this.prenom = p;] means that the field [prenom] of the current object ([this]) is assigned the value [p]. The keyword [this] refers to the current object: the one on which the method is executed. How do we know this? Let’s look at how the object referenced by [p1] is initialized in the calling program: [p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);]. It is the method [initialise] of the object [p1] that is called. When, within this method, the object [this] is referenced, it actually refers to the object [p1].

    When a method of an object references a field [a] of that object, the notation [this.a] is implied: the method [initialise] could have written [prenom = p;] and [nom = n;]. You must use [this] explicitly when there is a conflict of identifiers. This is the case with the statement [this.age = age;] (line 11), where [age] refers to both a field of the current object and the parameter [age] received by the method. In the method, the name [age] alone refers to the parameter; the field must be referred to as [this.age].

    4.1.8. Compact source files

    For a short example, a folder containing multiple files is unnecessarily large. As in the previous chapter, we will therefore write a compact source file (Java 25): a file that contains the method [void main()], possibly other methods and fields, and the classes the program needs. We run it with the source code launcher: [java Classes01.java].

    It is important to understand how the compiler processes such a file. It wraps it in an implicit class, which bears the file’s name ([Classes01]): the file’s methods and fields become members of this class, and the classes declared in the file become nested classes of this implicit class. The explicit compilation of the file demonstrates this:

    1
2
3
4
    > javac -d classes Classes01.java
> ls classes
Classes01$Personne.class
Classes01.class

    The full name of the class [Personne] in the file [Classes01.java] is therefore [Classes01$Personne]. This has two consequences that we will encounter in the examples:

    • a class and the classes it contains share their private members: the [main] method in a compact file has access to the private fields of the classes in that file. To ensure that a private field is inaccessible from outside its class, you must, as in the [Personnes] folder, place the class in its own file;
    • A regular nested class is an internal class: its objects are bound to an object of the enclosing class. This is not apparent as long as the objects are created by methods in the file, but a static method (see the section on class members) cannot create them. We then declare the nested class [static]. Records and interfaces, discussed later, are always static.

    Finally, a compact file automatically imports all public classes from the [java.base] module: [List], [ArrayList], [BigDecimal], [Objects]… can be used there without the [import] clause. This is not the case for a regular file such as [Personne.java], as we will see.

    4.1.9. Another method is initialized: overloading

    Let’s continue to consider the class [Personne] and add a second method to it: [initialise]. The program [Classes01.java] is as follows:

    // overload of the initialize method
void main() {
    Personne p1 = new Personne();
    p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    p1.identifie();
    Personne p2 = new Personne();
    p2.initialise(p1);
    p2.identifie();
}

// the Person class is declared after the main method
class Personne {
     // attributes
    private String prenom = "";
    private String nom = "";
    private int age;

     // initialization using three values
    public void initialise(String p, String n, int age) {
        prenom = p;
        nom = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

     // initialization from another person
    public void initialise(Personne p) {
        prenom = p.prenom;
        nom = p.nom;
        age = p.age;
    }

     // the person's identity
    public void identifie() {
        IO.println("[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}
    • lines 2–9: the main program;
    • line 12: the class [Personne] is declared after the method [main]. It is not public: in a compact file, this is unnecessary;
    • lines 19–23: the [initialise] method from the previous paragraph;
    • lines 26–30: a second method, [initialise].

    We now have two methods named [initialise]: this is valid as long as they accept different parameters (in number or type). The method [initialise] is said to be overloaded. The compiler chooses which method to call based on the actual parameters: [p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] (line 4) calls the first one, and [p2.initialise(p1)] (line 7) calls the second one. The return type alone is not sufficient to distinguish between two methods: two methods with the same name and the same parameters that differ only in their return type would be rejected.

    The parameter of the second method is a reference ([p]) to a person. The fields of the person ([p]) are then assigned to the current object ([this]). Note that the method [initialise] has direct access to the fields of the object [p] even though they are private (lines 27–29). This is always true: a method of a class [C] has access to the private members of all objects of the same class [C].

    4.1.10. Constructors of the Person class

    A constructor is a method that bears the name of the class and is called when the object is created. It is generally used to initialize the object. It is a method that can accept parameters but does not return a value. Its declaration is not preceded by any type (not even [void]).

    If a class [C] has a constructor that accepts n parameters, the declaration and initialization of an object of this class can be done in the form [C objet = new C(arg1, arg2, ... argn);], or in two steps: [C objet;], followed later by [objet = new C(arg1, arg2, ... argn);].

    When a class [C] has one or more constructors, one of these constructors must be used to create an object of that class. If a class [C] has no constructors, it has a default constructor with no parameters that does nothing. The object’s fields then retain their initial values. This is what happened in the previous programs, where we had written [new Personne()].

    The program [Classes02.java] returns three constructors for class [Personne]:

    // constructors of the Person class
void main() {
    Personne p1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    p1.identifie();
    Personne p2 = new Personne(p1);
    p2.identifie();
    Personne p3 = new Personne();
    p3.identifie();
}

class Personne {
     // attributes
    private String prenom;
    private String nom;
    private int age;

     // main constructor
    public Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age) {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
    }

     // copy constructor: it calls the primary constructor
    public Personne(Personne p) {
        this(p.prenom, p.nom, p.age);
    }

     // parameterless constructor: it also calls the primary constructor
    public Personne() {
        this("?", "?", 0);
    }

     // person's identity
    public void identifie() {
        IO.println("[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}
    • lines 18–22: the “main” constructor initializes the three fields. Since its parameters have the same names as the fields, the fields are distinguished using [this];
    • lines 25–27: the copy constructor. The statement [this(p.prenom, p.nom, p.age);] calls the constructor of the same class, which accepts three parameters: [String], [String], and [int]. This is referred to as chained constructors. As a result, the initialization code is written only once;
    • lines 30–32: the parameterless constructor, which is also chained to the main constructor. Since the class has declared constructors, it no longer has a default constructor: if you want to be able to write [new Personne()], you must declare it;
    • lines 13–15: the fields are no longer initialized at the time of their declaration; all constructors, either directly or through chaining, assign a value to them.

    The call [this(...)] to another constructor can only be made within a constructor. Up to Java 24, it had to be the first statement; since Java 25, statements that do not use the object being constructed (to verify or prepare parameters, for example) may precede it. We could also have constructors call a method such as [initialise]; however, chaining is preferable: the initialization code is in a single location, and a constructor should not call a method that a derived class might override—we’ll see why.

    // object references
void main() {
     // p1
    Personne p1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    IO.print("p1="); p1.identifie();
     // p2 refers to the same object as p1
    Personne p2 = p1;
    IO.print("p2="); p2.identifie();
     // p3 refers to an object that is a copy of the object referred to by p1
    Personne p3 = new Personne(p1);
    IO.print("p3="); p3.identifie();
     // The state of the object referenced by p1 is changed
    p1.initialise("Micheline", "Benoît", 67);
    IO.print("p1="); p1.identifie();
     // Since p2 = p1, the object referenced by p2 has changed state
    IO.print("p2="); p2.identifie();
     // p3 does not reference the same object as p1: the object referenced by p3 has not changed
    IO.print("p3="); p3.identifie();
     // Are p1 and p2 the same reference? What about p1 and p3?
    IO.println("p1 == p2 : " + (p1 == p2) + ", p1 == p3 : " + (p1 == p3));
}

class Personne {
     // attributes
    private String prenom;
    private String nom;
    private int age;

     // constructors
    public Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age) {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public Personne(Personne p) {
        this(p.prenom, p.nom, p.age);
    }

     // initialization
    public void initialise(String p, String n, int age) {
        prenom = p;
        nom = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

     // person’s identity
    public void identifie() {
        IO.println("[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}

    The [IO.print] method (lines 5, 8, …) writes its parameter without wrapping to the next line. Results:

    1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8
    > java Classes03.java
p1=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p2=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p3=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p1=[Micheline, Benoît, 67]
p2=[Micheline, Benoît, 67]
p3=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p1 == p2 : true, p1 == p3 : false

    When the variable [p1] is declared via [Personne p1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);] (line 4), [p1] references the object [Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] but is not the object itself. In C, this would be referred to as a pointer—that is, the address of the created object. If we then write [p1 = null;], it is not the object [Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] that is modified; rather, it is the reference [p1] that changes its value. The object will be “lost” if it is not referenced by any other variable: the memory it occupies will later be reclaimed by the Java virtual machine’s garbage collector.

    When we write [Personne p2 = p1;] (line 7), we initialize the reference [p2]: it “points” to the same object (it refers to the same object) as the reference [p1]. Thus, if the object “pointed to” (or referenced) by [p1] is modified, the object referenced by [p2] is also modified (lines 5–6 of the results).

    When [Personne p3 = new Personne(p1);] is written (line 10), a new object, [Personne], is created. This new object will be referenced by [p3]. If you modify the object referenced by [p1], you do not modify the one referenced by [p3] (line 7 of the results).

    Finally, on line 20, the operator [==], applied to two object references, indicates whether they refer to the same object: [p1] and [p2] refer to the same object, while [p1] and [p3] refer to two different objects, although they have the same content (line 8 of the results). We will see later how to compare the contents of two objects using the [equals] method.

    4.1.12. Passing Object Reference Parameters

    In the previous chapter, we saw that Java passes method parameters by value: the method receives a copy of the actual parameter’s value. Let’s see what this means when the parameter is an object reference. To do this, we’ll use the [StringBuilder] class from JDK. A [String] object cannot be modified: an operation such as [s.toUpperCase()] returns a new [String] object. A [StringBuilder] object, on the other hand, is a mutable string: its [append] method adds characters to the string without creating a new object.

    The program [Classes04.java] is as follows:

    // passing parameters of the object reference type
void main() {
    StringBuilder sb0 = new StringBuilder("essai0"), sb1 = new StringBuilder("essai1");
    IO.println("Dans fonction appelante avant appel : sb0=" + sb0 + ", sb1=" + sb1);
    StringBuilder sb2 = changeStringBuilder(sb0, sb1);
    IO.println("Dans fonction appelante après appel : sb0=" + sb0 + ", sb1=" + sb1 + ", sb2=" + sb2);
}

// the called function
StringBuilder changeStringBuilder(StringBuilder sbf0, StringBuilder sbf1) {
    IO.println("Début fonction appelée : sbf0=" + sbf0 + ", sbf1=" + sbf1);
     // the object referenced by sbf0 is modified
    sbf0.append("*****");
     // sbf1 now references a new object
    sbf1 = new StringBuilder("essai1*****");
     // a new object is returned to the caller
    StringBuilder sbf2 = new StringBuilder("essai2*****");
    IO.println("Fin fonction appelée : sbf0=" + sbf0 + ", sbf1=" + sbf1 + ", sbf2=" + sbf2);
    return sbf2;
}
    • line 3: two references, [sb0] and [sb1], to objects of type [StringBuilder];
    • line 5: these are passed to the method [changeStringBuilder], whose result—a third reference—is assigned to [sb2];
    • lines 10–20: a method in the compact file, which has the formal parameters [sbf0] and [sbf1]. When the method starts, [sbf0] and [sb0] are two distinct references that point to the same object: the reference [sb0] was copied into [sbf0] (references are passed by value). The same applies to [sbf1] and [sb1].

    Explanations:

    • [sb0] and [sbf0] are two distinct references to the same object. This object was modified via [sbf0] (line 13). This modification is visible via [sb0] (line 5 of the results);
    • [sb1] and [sbf1] are two distinct references to the same object. [sbf1] is assigned a new value in the method and now points to a new object (line 15). This does not change the value of [sb1], which continues to point to the original, unmodified object;
    • a Java method cannot, therefore, change the value of a caller’s variable. To pass a new object back to the caller, it returns it as a result (lines 17 and 19). When there are multiple results, they are grouped into an object, such as a record (see below).

    Keep in mind that a method can modify the object referenced by a parameter, but not the caller’s variable that contains the reference. Unlike other languages such as C#, Java does not support passing parameters by reference.

    4.1.13. Temporary Objects

    In an expression, you can explicitly call an object’s constructor: the object is created, but there is no variable to access it later (to modify it, for example). This temporary object is created for the purpose of evaluating the expression and is then discarded. The memory space it occupied will later be automatically reclaimed by the garbage collector, whose role is to reclaim memory space occupied by objects that are no longer referenced by the program’s data.

    The names of these methods follow a convention established since the early days of Java, namely “JavaBeans”: the getter for the field [age] is named [getAge], and its setter is named [setAge]; the getter for a boolean field named [actif] is instead called [isActif]. Many libraries (such as Jackson for JSON and Hibernate for databases, which we’ll use later) rely on this convention to retrieve an object’s data. Unlike other languages such as C#, Java does not have “properties”: accessing an object’s state always involves methods, or—for immutable objects—records, which we’ll cover later. Development environments can generate getters and setters from fields (in IntelliJ and IDEA, under the “Code / Generate…” menu).

void main() {
    Personne p = new Personne("Jean", "Michelin", 34);
    IO.println("p=(" + p.getPrenom() + "," + p.getNom() + "," + p.getAge() + ")");
    p.setAge(56);
    IO.println("p=(" + p.getPrenom() + "," + p.getNom() + "," + p.getAge() + ")");
    try {
        p.setAge(-4);
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        IO.println(ex.getMessage());
    }
     // parameterless constructor followed by a call to modifiers
    Personne p2 = new Personne();
    p2.setAge(7);
    p2.setPrenom("Arthur");
    p2.setNom("Martin");
    IO.println("p2=(" + p2.getPrenom() + "," + p2.getNom() + "," + p2.getAge() + ")");
    try {
        Personne p3 = new Personne();
        p3.setPrenom("Paul");
        p3.setNom(" ");
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        IO.println(ex.getMessage());
    }
}

class Personne {
     // attributes
    private String prenom = "";
    private String nom = "";
    private int age;

     // constructors
    public Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age) {
         // We use modifiers to take advantage of their validations
        setPrenom(prenom);
        setNom(nom);
        setAge(age);
    }

    public Personne() {
    }

     // accessors
    public String getPrenom() {
        return prenom;
    }

    public String getNom() {
        return nom;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

     // modifiers: they are declared `final` because the constructor calls them
    public final void setPrenom(String prenom) {
         // Is the first name valid?
        if (prenom == null || prenom.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("prénom (" + prenom + ") invalide");
        }
        this.prenom = prenom;
    }

    public final void setNom(String nom) {
         // Is the last name valid?
        if (nom == null || nom.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("nom (" + nom + ") invalide");
        }
        this.nom = nom;
    }

    public final void setAge(int age) {
         // Is the age valid?
        if (age < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("âge (" + age + ") invalide");
        }
        this.age = age;
    }
}

    The three modifiers validate the received value (lines 60–62, 68–70, 76–78).

    • Lines 60–62: The method [isBlank] (Java 11) returns [true] if the string is empty or consists solely of spaces. The [prenom == null] test is performed first: if [prenom] is equal to [null], the operator [||] does not evaluate its second operand, which would cause a [NullPointerException] exception. The exception thrown is of type [IllegalArgumentException], the exception provided by Java to signal an invalid parameter. This is an uncaught exception: the method does not need to declare it with [throws];
    • lines 34–39: the constructor initializes the object using accessors rather than fields. This allows it to take advantage of the validations performed by the accessors, which are written in only one place;
    • lines 58, 66, 74: the modifiers are declared as [final]. We will see with inheritance that a derived class can override the methods of its parent class; the keyword [final] prevents this. Without it, a derived class could redefine [setAge], and the constructor of [Personne] would call this new version even before the derived class’s constructor has been executed. The compiler, with the [-Xlint:all] option, flags this risk (warning [this-escape]) for a public class written in its own file;
    • lines 41–42: a parameterless constructor, which leaves the fields at their initial values.

    Unlike other languages, Java does not have an object initializer—a syntax that would allow multiple fields to be set within the [new] expression itself: instead, as shown here, we chain the constructor and setter calls, or we write a constructor that takes all the values. We’ll look at two other solutions: “fluid” modifiers and records.

void main() {
    Personne p = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30, "Angers");
    IO.println(p.getIdentite());
     // first name is read/write
    p.setPrenom("Jacques");

    p.vieillir();
    IO.println(p.getIdentite());
     // The following lines are rejected by the compiler
     // p.setNom("Durand  "); // there is no modifier for the name

     // p.ville = "Pari   s"; // the city field is the last one

    Contact c = new Contact("jean.dupont@exemple.fr");

class Personne {
     // fields
    private String prenom;
     // final fields: they are assigned their values once and for all in the constructor
    private final String nom;
    private final String ville;
    private int age;

     // constructor
    public Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age, String ville) {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
        this.ville = ville;
    }

     // first name (read/write)
    public String getPrenom() {
        return prenom;
    }

    public void setPrenom(String prenom) {
        this.prenom = prenom;
    }

     // last name, age, and city (read-only)
    public String getNom() {
        return nom;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

    public String getVille() {
        return ville;
    }

     // a calculated value
    public String getIdentite() {
        return "[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + ", " + ville + "]";
    }

     // Age can only be modified by the class's methods
    public void vieillir() {
        age++;
    }
}

class Contact {
     // Email is required; phone number is optional
    private final String email;
    private final String telephone;

     // constructor with both values
    public Contact(String email, String telephone) {
        this.email = Objects.requireNonNull(email, "l'email est obligatoire");
        this.telephone = telephone;
    }

     // constructor without the phone number: default value
    public Contact(String email) {
        this(email, "inconnu");
    }

    public String getEmail() {
        return email;
    }

    public String getTelephone() {
        return telephone;
    }
}
    • lines 28 and 43–49: the first name is both read-only and writable; it has a getter and a setter;
    • lines 30–31: the last name and city are [final] fields. The constructor assigns a value to them (lines 37 and 39), which cannot be changed afterward;
    • line 32 and lines 56–58: The age is readable by everyone but does not have a public setter; it can only be modified by the class’s methods, such as [vieillir] (lines 70–72);
    • lines 65–67: the method [getIdentite] returns a value calculated from the fields. To the user of the class, it is indistinguishable from an accessor;
    • lines 11–13: three statements that the compiler rejects, for the reasons given in the comments. For the third one, the compiler’s message is: [cannot assign a value to final variable ville];
    • Lines 75–98: The [Contact] class has one required field—email—and one optional field—phone. The required field is enforced by the constructor: a [Contact] object cannot be created without an email address. The [Objects.requireNonNull(valeur, message)] method (line 82) returns its first parameter if it is not [null] and throws a [NullPointerException] exception with the specified message otherwise: An email address of the form [null] is rejected (lines 18–23);
    • lines 87–89: the optional nature of the phone number is expressed through a second constructor, which provides a default value. Java does not have optional parameters: we overload the constructor.

    Note that in a compact file, the method [main] has access to the private fields of the file’s classes: this is why the comments on lines 11–13 do not rely on the private nature of the fields, but rather on the absence of a modifier and on the keyword [final].

    // "Fluid" modifiers: they make the object current
void main() {
    Personne p = new Personne().setPrenom("  jean ").setNom("Dupont").setAge(30);
    IO.println(p.getIdentite());
    try {
        p.setNom("");
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        IO.println(ex.getMessage());
    }
    try {
        p.setAge(-4);
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        IO.println(ex.getMessage());
    }
    IO.println(p.getIdentite());
}

class Personne {
     // fields
    private String prenom = "";
    private String nom = "";
    private int age;

     // fluid modifiers: each one makes the object current (this)
    public Personne setPrenom(String prenom) {
        this.prenom = verifier(prenom, "prénom");
        return this;
    }

    public Personne setNom(String nom) {
        this.nom = verifier(nom, "nom");
        return this;
    }

    public Personne setAge(int age) {
        if (age < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("âge (" + age + ") invalide");
        }
        this.age = age;
        return this;
    }

     // identity
    public String getIdentite() {
        return "[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]";
    }

     // checking for a required string: it is returned without its leading and trailing spaces
    private static String verifier(String valeur, String libelle) {
        if (valeur == null || valeur.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(libelle + " (" + valeur + ") invalide");
        }
        return valeur.strip();
    }
}
    • lines 25–28: the modifier [setPrenom] checks the received value, assigns it to the field, and returns the current object. Its return type is therefore [Personne];
    • line 3: the calls are chained: [new Personne()] returns a person, on which [setPrenom] is called, which returns the same person, on which [setNom] is called, and so on. The syntax resembles an object initializer;
    • Lines 49–54: The checks for the first name and last name, which are identical, are factored into the private method [verifier]. It is declared as [static] because it does not use any fields of the object (static members are discussed in the following paragraph). The method [strip] (Java 11) removes the leading and trailing spaces from the string.

    The first name “jean,” provided with spaces on either side (line 3), was stored without them (line 2 of the results). Fluid modifiers do not follow the JavaBeans convention, according to which a modifier returns nothing ([void]): some libraries do not recognize them. To construct complex objects, the “Builder” design pattern is also used: an auxiliary class, equipped with fluid methods, collects the values and then constructs the final object, which can then be immutable.

    4.1.18. Class Methods and Attributes

    Suppose we want to count the number of [Personne] objects created in an application. We could manage a counter ourselves, but we risk overlooking temporary objects that are created here and there. It seems safer to include an instruction in the constructors of the [Personne] class that increments a counter. This counter cannot be an ordinary field, since each object has its own fields: it is a field of the class itself and not that of a particular instance of that class. It is declared using the keyword [static]: [private static long nbPersonnes;].

    To refer to it, we write [Personne.nbPersonnes] to indicate that it is a field of the [Personne] class itself. Here, we have created a private field that cannot be accessed directly from outside the class. We therefore create a public accessor to provide access to the class field [nbPersonnes]. To retrieve the value of *[nbPersonnes]*, this accessor does not require a specific *[Personne] object; therefore, we also declare it as *[static]. From the outside, it will be called using the syntax [Personne.getNbPersonnes()]. Here is an example of [Classes10.java]:

void main() {
    Personne p1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    Personne p2 = new Personne(p1);
    new Personne(p1);
    IO.println("Nombre de personnes créées : " + Personne.getNbPersonnes());

    Personne p3 = Personne.inconnue();
    p3.identifie();
    IO.println("Nombre de personnes créées : " + Personne.getNbPersonnes());
}

// static nested class: see explanations
static class Personne {
     // class attribute
    private static long nbPersonnes;

     // class accessor
    public static long getNbPersonnes() {
        return nbPersonnes;
    }

     // class method
    public static Personne inconnue() {
        return new Personne("?", "?", 0);
    }

     // instance attributes
    private String prenom;
    private String nom;
    private int age;

     // constructors
    public Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age) {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
        nbPersonnes++;
    }

    public Personne(Personne p) {
        this(p.prenom, p.nom, p.age);
    }

     // person ID
    public void identifie() {
        IO.println("[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}
    • line 16: the class field. Like any numeric field, it is initialized to 0;
    • lines 19–21: the class accessor;
    • lines 24–26: a class method. It is called using the class name: [Personne.inconnue()] (line 8). A class method has no current object: the keyword [this] has no meaning there, and it can only directly use the class members [static]. A static method that creates and returns an object of its class, such as this one, is called a static factory;
    • line 38: the primary constructor increments the counter. The copy constructor, which is chained to the primary constructor, therefore increments it as well;
    • Line 14: The class [Personne] is declared as [static]. As explained in the section on compact files: a class declared in a compact file is a nested class of the implicit class. Without the [static] keyword, it is an internal class, where each object is bound to an object of the enclosing class; the static method [inconnue], which has no current object, would be unable to create one, and the compiler would report the error [non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context]. A class written in its own file does not have this problem.

[?, ?, 0]

    The program correctly counted the temporary object created on line 5. We have been using class members from the beginning: [IO.println], [Integer.parseInt], [Math.sqrt] are methods, [static] and [Math.PI] are methods, and [static] is a field. The class [Math] contains only static members: it is declared as [final], and its sole constructor is private, which prevents the creation of instances. This is the Java way of writing a utility class.

    4.2. Inheritance by Example

    4.2.1. Overview

    Here we introduce the concept of inheritance. The purpose of inheritance is to “customize” an existing class so that it meets our needs. Suppose we want to create a class [Enseignant]: a teacher is a specific type of person. They have attributes that other people do not have: the subject they teach, for example. But they also have the attributes common to all people: first name, last name, and age. A teacher is therefore a full member of the class [Personne] but has additional attributes. Rather than creating a class [Enseignant] from scratch, we prefer to build upon the existing class [Personne] and adapt it to the specific characteristics of teachers. This is made possible by the concept of inheritance.

    To indicate that the class [Enseignant] inherits from the class [Personne], we write [public class Enseignant extends Personne].

    [Personne] is called the parent class (or base class, or superclass), and [Enseignant] is called the derived class (or child class, or subclass). A [Enseignant] object has all the properties of a [Personne] object: it has the same fields and methods. These fields and methods from the parent class are not repeated in the definition of the child class; we simply specify the fields and methods added by the child class. A Java class can inherit from only one parent class.

    public class Personne {
     // class field: the number of people created
    private static long nbPersonnes;

     // instance fields
    private String prenom;
    private String nom;
    private int age;

     // constructor
    public Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age) {
        setPrenom(prenom);
        setNom(nom);
        setAge(age);
        nbPersonnes++;
        IO.println("Constructeur Personne(String, String, int)");
    }

     // number of people created
    public static long getNbPersonnes() {
        return nbPersonnes;
    }

     // accessors
    public String getPrenom() {
        return prenom;
    }

    public String getNom() {
        return nom;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

     // modifiers
    public final void setPrenom(String prenom) {
        this.prenom = verifier(prenom, "prénom");
    }

    public final void setNom(String nom) {
        this.nom = verifier(nom, "nom");
    }

    public final void setAge(int age) {
        if (age < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("âge (" + age + ") invalide");
        }
        this.age = age;
    }

     // person's identity
    public String getIdentite() {
        return "[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]";
    }

     // validation of a required string
    private static String verifier(String valeur, String libelle) {
        if (valeur == null || valeur.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(libelle + " (" + valeur + ") invalide");
        }
        return valeur;
    }
}

    4.2.2. Creating a Teacher Object

    A child class does not inherit constructors from its parent class. It must define its own constructors. The constructor for the [Enseignant] class is as follows:

    1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8
        public Enseignant(String prenom, String nom, int age, int section) {
         // constructing the "Person" part of the object
        super(prenom, nom, age);
         // the section is stored
        this.section = section;
         // follow-up
        IO.println("Constructeur Enseignant(String, String, int, int)");
    }

    The constructor receives four parameters ([prenom], [nom], [age], [section]) and passes three ([prenom], [nom], [age]) to its parent class—in this case, the class [Personne]—using the statement [super(prenom, nom, age);] (line 3). We know that this class has a constructor, [Personne(String, String, int)], which will be used to create a person with the passed parameters. Once the construction of the [Personne] part is complete, the construction of the [Enseignant] object continues by executing the rest of the constructor (lines 5–7).

    In summary, the constructor of a derived class:

    • passes to its parent class, via [super(...)], the parameters that the parent class needs to construct itself;
    • uses the other parameters to initialize its own fields.

    We could have chosen to initialize the fields [prenom], [nom], and [age] directly in the constructor of class [Enseignant], using statements like [this.prenom = prenom;]. This is impossible for two reasons. First, the private fields [prenom], [nom], and [age] are accessible only to methods of the [Personne] class. All other objects, including objects of derived classes as in this case, must access them through public (or protected) members. This would have been different if the class *[Personne] had declared these fields as protected (*[protected]*): it would then have allowed derived classes to access them directly. Furthermore, the [Personne] part of the object must in any case be constructed by a constructor of the [Personne] class: in the absence of a call to [super(...)], the compiler inserts a call to [super()]—the parameterless constructor of the parent class. However, the class [Personne] does not have one. If the [super(prenom, nom, age);]* statement is removed, the compiler reports the following error:

    1
2

    > java Main.java
.../Heritage1/Enseignant.java:6: error: constructor Personne in class Personne cannot be applied to given types;
    public Enseignant(String prenom, String nom, int age, int section) {
                                                                       ^
  required: String,String,int
  found:    no arguments
  reason: actual and formal argument lists differ in length
1 error
error: compilation failed

    Using the parent class’s constructor is therefore the correct solution and the standard approach: when constructing a child object, first call the parent object’s constructor, then complete the initializations specific to the child object ([section] in our example). As with [this(...)], only statements that do not use the object being constructed may precede the call to [super(...)] (since Java 25; previously, [super(...)] had to be the first statement).

    4.2.4. Polymorphism

    Consider a class hierarchy: C0 ← C1 ← C2 ← … ← Cn, where Ci ← Cj indicates that class Cj is derived from class Ci. This implies that class Cj has all the characteristics of class Ci plus additional ones. Let Oi be objects of type Ci. It is valid to write [Oi = Oj] with j > i. Indeed, by inheritance, class Cj has all the characteristics of class Ci plus additional ones. Therefore, an object Oj of type Cj contains an object of type Ci. The operation [Oi = Oj] causes the variable Oi, of type Ci, to reference the object Oj: only the members defined in class Ci can be accessed through it.

    The fact that a variable Oi of class Ci can actually reference not only an object of class Ci but any object derived from class Ci is called polymorphism: the ability of a variable to reference different types of objects.

    Let’s take an example and consider the method [affiche] from the previous program:

    1
2
3
    void affiche(Personne p) {
    IO.println(p.getIdentite());
}

    We can pass it either a *[Personne] or a *[Enseignant]: In the latter case, the formal parameter [p], which is of type [Personne], receives a value of type [Enseignant]. Since the type [Enseignant] is derived from the type [Personne], this is valid. The [p.getIdentite()] statement here executed the [getIdentite] method of the [Personne] class, the only one that exists in the program: for the teacher (line 7 of the results), we only get the identity of its “Person” part. Let’s see what happens when the class [Enseignant] has its own method [getIdentite].

    // a final class: cannot be derived from
public final class Enseignant extends Personne {
     // Field specific to the Teacher class
    private int section;

     // constructor

It relies on the method [getIdentite] from its parent class, referred to as [super.getIdentite()], to retrieve the “Person” portion, then supplements it with the section specific to the class [Enseignant];
    • Line 23: The annotation [@Override] tells the compiler that the method intends to override a method of the parent class. It is not mandatory, but it is strongly recommended: if the method did not override anything (due to a typo in the name or different parameters), the compiler would report the error instead of silently creating a new method;
    • Line 2: The class is final ([final]), which we’ll explain in more detail later.

    Consider a teacher object [E]. This object contains a [Personne] object within it:

    The method [getIdentite] is defined in both the class [Enseignant] and its parent class [Personne]. In Java, all instance methods that are neither private nor final can be overridden, and the choice of which method is executed by [p.getIdentite()] is made at runtime, based on the actual type of the object referenced by [p], rather than at compile time based on the declared type of the variable. This is known as dynamic binding. To execute [o.m()], the virtual machine searches for a method named [m] in the following order:

    • in the class of the [o] object;
    • in its parent class, if it has one;
    • in the parent class of its parent class, if it exists;
    • and so on.

    Inheritance therefore allows you to redefine methods in the child class that have the same signature as those in the parent class. This is what enables you to adapt the child class to its own needs. The program [Main.java] in the folder [Heritage2] is as follows:

Unlike other languages such as C#, where a method can only be overridden if it is declared virtual, Java methods are “virtual” by default; there is no such thing as overriding an instance method.

    4.2.6. The Object class and the toString method

    The [java.lang.Object] class is the “parent” class of all Java classes. Thus, when you write [public class Personne], you are implicitly writing [public class Personne extends Object].

    The [Object] class defines several methods that all objects inherit:

    • [String toString()]: returns a textual representation of the object. By default, this is the object’s class name, followed by the character [@] and a hash code written in hexadecimal;
    • [boolean equals(Object o)]: indicates whether the object is “equal” to the object [o]. By default, it is equal only to itself: the method compares references, like the operator [==];
    • [int hashCode()]: returns a hash code for the object, used by dictionaries and sets (see the next chapter). The methods [equals] and [hashCode] are discussed later;
    • [Class<?> getClass()]: returns the description of the object’s actual class. The method [getSimpleName] in this description returns the class name, while [getName] returns its full name.

    It is the method [toString] of the class [Object] that was used by the calls [e.toString()] and [p.toString()] in the file [Heritage1]: [Enseignant@70325e14] and [Personne@37ceb1df] (lines 9–10 of the results; the numbers vary from one execution to another). Although we did not redefine the method [toString] in the classes [Personne] and [Enseignant], the method [toString] in the class [Object] was able to display the actual class name of the object.

    In the [Heritage2] folder, the [Personne] class redefines the [toString] method (see above). Let’s return to the program [Main.java] in the folder [Heritage2]:

         // IO.println(Object) displays the result of the toString method of the object
    IO.println(e);
    IO.println(p);
     // an array of people of different types
    Personne[] personnes = { p, e };
    for (Personne personne : personnes) {
        IO.println(personne.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + personne);
    }

    Line 2: The [IO.println(Object)] method accepts a parameter of type [Object]; therefore, since [Object] is the superclass of all classes, any object—in this case, a [Enseignant]—can be passed. It prints the result of the object’s [toString] method to the console. Since the binding is dynamic, the [toString] method of the actual object is used—in this case, the one inherited from the [Personne] class. This returns [getIdentite()], a redefined method: For the teacher [e], the method [getIdentite] from the class [Enseignant] is therefore executed, as shown in line 9 of the results. It is therefore unnecessary to redefine [toString] in the class [Enseignant].

    The same mechanism applies to the concatenation of a string and an object: in [" : " + personne] (line 7), the object [personne] is converted to a string by its method [toString]. The loop in lines 6–8 iterates over an array of references [Personne] that actually point to objects of different types: [getClass().getSimpleName()] returns the actual class name of each object (lines 11–12 of the results).

    4.2.7. Final classes and sealed classes

    The class [Enseignant] in the package [Heritage2] is declared as [public final class Enseignant extends Personne]. The keyword [final] prevents classes from being derived from the class [Enseignant]: the declaration [class EnseignantChercheur extends Enseignant] would be rejected by the compiler. A class is marked as final when it is not intended to be derived from. We have seen that the keyword also applies to methods: a method named [final] cannot be overridden by derived classes without prohibiting derivation from that class. For example, the class [String], derived from JDK, is final.

    Between a class open to all derivations and a final class, Java 17 has added an intermediate option: the sealed class ([sealed]), which provides an exhaustive list of its direct derived classes. The program [Classes13.java] illustrates this:

    // final classes and sealed classes (Java 17)
void main() {
    Personne[] personnes = {
        new Enseignant("Lucile", "Dumas", 61),
        new Etudiant("Paul", "Martin", "informatique"),
        new Vacataire("Marc", "Petit"),
        new Intervenant("Lise", "Morel", "Airbus"),
    };
    for (Personne p : personnes) {
        IO.println(p.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + p.getIdentite());
    }
     // the permitted direct subclasses of the sealed class Person
    IO.println("Personne est scellée : " + Personne.class.isSealed());
    for (Class<?> c : Personne.class.getPermittedSubclasses()) {
        IO.println("sous-classe autorisée : " + c.getSimpleName());
    }
}

// A sealed class: only the classes listed after "permits" may be derived from it
abstract sealed class Personne permits Enseignant, Etudiant, Vacataire {
    private final String prenom;
    private final String nom;

    protected Personne(String prenom, String nom) {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
    }

    public String getIdentite() {
        return "[" + prenom + ", " + nom + "]";
    }
}

// A class derived from a sealed class must be final, sealed, or non-sealed
final class Enseignant extends Personne {
    private final int section;

    public Enseignant(String prenom, String nom, int section) {
        super(prenom, nom);
        this.section = section;
    }

    @Override
    public String getIdentite() {
        return super.getIdentite() + ", section " + section;
    }
}

final class Etudiant extends Personne {
    private final String filiere;

    public Etudiant(String prenom, String nom, String filiere) {
        super(prenom, nom);
        this.filiere = filiere;
    }

    @Override
    public String getIdentite() {
        return super.getIdentite() + ", filière " + filiere;
    }
}

// non-sealed: the hierarchy is open again starting from this class
non-sealed class Vacataire extends Personne {
    public Vacataire(String prenom, String nom) {
        super(prenom, nom);
    }
}

// A class derived from "Vacataire": allowed, since "Vacataire" is not sealed
class Intervenant extends Vacataire {
    private final String entreprise;

    public Intervenant(String prenom, String nom, String entreprise) {
        super(prenom, nom);
        this.entreprise = entreprise;
    }

    @Override
    public String getIdentite() {
        return super.getIdentite() + ", entreprise " + entreprise;
    }
}

// Rejected by the compiler: `Artist` is not listed in the `permits` clause of `Person`
// final class Artist extends Person { ... }
    • Line 20: The abstract class (see below: you cannot create objects of this class, only of its derived classes) [Personne] is sealed. Only the classes [Enseignant], [Etudiant], and [Vacataire], listed after the keyword [permits], can be derived from it. When derived classes are declared in the same file, as here, the [permits] clause may be omitted: the authorized classes are then those in the file that are directly derived from it. In a larger program, the authorized classes must belong to the same package as the sealed class (or to the same module if the sealed class belongs to a named module);
    • line 24: the constructor is protected ([protected]): it is intended only for derived classes;
    • Lines 35 and 49: A class derived from a sealed class must specify how it itself can be derived. The classes [Enseignant] and [Etudiant] are final;
    • line 64: the class [Vacataire] is declared as [non-sealed]: this reopens the hierarchy, allowing any class to derive from it. A third option is to declare it as [sealed] itself, with its own list of permitted classes;
    • lines 71–83: The class [Intervenant] derives from [Vacataire], which is allowed;
    • lines 85–86: a class [Artiste] derived from [Personne] would be rejected;
    • Lines 13–16: The description of a class ([Personne.class]) indicates whether it is sealed ([isSealed]) and lists its authorized direct derived classes ([getPermittedSubclasses]).

    What is the purpose of a sealed class? It allows the author of a class hierarchy to maintain control over it: the author knows that any [Personne] is a [Enseignant], a [Etudiant], or a [Vacataire]. The compiler knows this as well and uses it in pattern filtering, which is discussed at the end of the chapter: a [switch] that handles all three cases is complete. The mechanism also applies to interfaces ([sealed interface]), which are discussed later.

    4.3. No operator overloading: equals, compareTo…

    Some languages, such as C# or C++, allow you to redefine the meaning of operators ([+], [==], [<]…) for a class. Java does not allow this: operators always have the meaning assigned to them by the language. The only exception is the [+] operator applied to a string, which performs concatenation and uses the [toString] method of the concatenated object to do so. Instead of operators, we write methods that follow well-established conventions:

    Operation
    Java Method
    Example
    Content equality ([==] compares references)
    [boolean equals(Object o)], inherited from [Object]
    [s1.equals(s2)]
    Comparison ([<], [>]…)
    [int compareTo(T autre)] from the [Comparable<T>] interface: negative, null, or positive result
    [s1.compareTo(s2) < 0]
    arithmetic operations
    explicitly named methods
    [a.add(b)], [a.multiply(b)] for [BigDecimal]
    Addition to a collection ([+=])
    [add]
    [liste.add(p)]

    4.3.1. An example

    The folder [Listes] contains a class [ListeDePersonnes], a list of people, whose methods act as the operators [+] and [+=]. The classes [Personne] and [Enseignant] in this folder are simplified versions of those in the [Heritage2] folder: the fields are [final] and have no modifiers; there are no longer any tracking messages or counters. The people are organized into a generic list [List<Personne>] (generic classes are discussed later in this chapter; lists are covered in the next chapter). Rather than having the class [ListeDePersonnes] inherit from a list class derived from JDK, we place the list in a private field of the class. This is referred to as using composition rather than inheritance: the class [ListeDePersonnes] thus exposes only the operations it has chosen. From the interface [List<Personne>], we use only the following elements:

    • the method [l.add(p)], which adds the person [p] to the list [l], and the [l.addAll(l2)] method, which adds all elements from the [l2] list to it;
    • the method [l.size()], which returns the number of elements in the list [l];
    • the methods [l.get(i)] and [l.set(i, p)], which read and modify element number i of the list [l].

    import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.StringJoiner;

public class ListeDePersonnes {
     // the people on the list
    private final List<Personne> personnes = new ArrayList<>();

     // number of people in the list
    public int size() {
        return personnes.size();
    }

     // the equivalent of a + operator: returns a new list containing the people
     // from the current list and person p
    public ListeDePersonnes plus(Personne p) {
        ListeDePersonnes resultat = new ListeDePersonnes();
        resultat.personnes.addAll(personnes);
        resultat.personnes.add(p);
        return resultat;
    }

     // the equivalent of a += operator: adds p to the current list, which is then returned
    public ListeDePersonnes ajouter(Personne p) {
        personnes.add(p);
        return this;
    }

     // the equivalent of an indexer: reads and writes element number i
    public Personne get(int i) {
        return personnes.get(i);
    }

    public void set(int i, Personne p) {
        personnes.set(i, p);
    }

     // position of the person with the specified name; -1 if they do not exist
    public int indexOf(String nom) {
        for (int i = 0; i < personnes.size(); i++) {
            if (personnes.get(i).getNom().equals(nom)) {
                return i;
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }

     // toString: returns (person1, person2, ...)
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner(",", "(", ")");
        for (Personne p : personnes) {
            joiner.add(p.toString());
        }
        return joiner.toString();
    }
}
    • lines 1–3: Unlike the compact file [Main.java], a regular file does not automatically import the classes from the [java.base] module: it must import the ones it uses (except for those from the [java.lang] package, such as [String], which are always known). The [import] clauses are provided with the packages;
    • line 7: the list of people. The keyword [final] indicates that the field will always refer to the same list; the list itself may change in content. [new ArrayList<>()] creates an empty list; the “diamond” operator [<>] allows the compiler to infer the type of the elements, [Personne], from the field type;
    • lines 10–12: the number of people;
    • lines 16–21: the method [plus] acts as a [+] operator for the operation [l.plus(p)], where [l] is of type [ListeDePersonnes] and [p] is of type [Personne] or a derivative thereof. It creates a new list (line 17), copies the people from the current list into it (line 18), and then adds the person [p] (line 19). As with the [+] operator for numbers or strings, the operands are not modified. Since the list [resultat] is of the same class, the method has access to its private field [resultat.personnes]. The returned list is of type [ListeDePersonnes], which allows for chained calls as in [l.plus(p1).plus(p2)];
    • lines 24–27: the method [ajouter] acts as a [+=] operator: it modifies the current list by adding the person [p] to it and returns that same list, which also allows for chained calls;
    • Lines 49–56: We redefine the [toString] method to display a list of people in the form (person1, person2, ...), where personi is itself the result of the person’s [toString] method. A [StringJoiner] object (line 51) constructs a string from successive elements ([add], line 53), separating them with the specified separator (in this case, a comma) and enclosing them with a prefix and a suffix (in this case, parentheses).

    Note that the class [ListeDePersonnes] has no constructor. It therefore uses the default constructor, which takes no parameters and does nothing other than initialize the field [personnes] with the value specified in its declaration. Lines 29–46 are discussed in the following section.

    void main() {
     // --- methods instead of operators
    String s1 = "jean";
    String s2 = new StringBuilder("je").append("an").toString();
    IO.println("s1 == s2 : " + (s1 == s2) + ", s1.equals(s2) : " + s1.equals(s2));
    IO.println("s1.compareTo(\"paul\") : " + s1.compareTo("paul"));
    BigDecimal a = new BigDecimal("0.10"), b = new BigDecimal("0.20");
    IO.println("a + b = " + a.add(b) + ", a < b : " + (a.compareTo(b) < 0));

     // --- the plus method
     // a list of people
    ListeDePersonnes l = new ListeDePersonnes();
     // adding people
    l = l.plus(new Personne("jean", "martin", 10)).plus(new Personne("pauline", "leduc", 12));
     // display
    IO.println("l=" + l);
     // l.plus(p) returns a new list: l remains unchanged
    ListeDePersonnes l2 = l.plus(new Personne("louis", "durand", 8));
    IO.println("l=" + l);
    IO.println("l2=" + l2);

     // --- the add method
    ListeDePersonnes l3 = l;
     // add modifies the list referenced by l, without creating a new list
    l.ajouter(new Enseignant("camille", "germain", 27, 60));
    IO.println("l=" + l);
     // `l` and `l3` still refer to the same object
    IO.println("l3 == l : " + (l3 == l));

    • line 6: the method [compareTo] returns a negative number because “jean” comes before “paul” in the character code order;
    • Lines 7–8: The class [BigDecimal] (exact decimal numbers, which we will use for the amounts) replaces the operators [+] and [<] with the methods [add] and [compareTo];
    • line 12: creation of an empty list of people [l];
    • line 14: Add two people using the [plus] method;
    • line 18: [l.plus(p)] creates a new list, [l2]; the list [l] remains unchanged;
    • line 25: adds a teacher using the [ajouter] method;
    • lines 16–20: concatenating a string and an object uses the [toString] method, which is redefined from the [ListeDePersonnes] class.

    Why are there two methods, when [l = l.plus(p)] produces the same output as [l.ajouter(p)]? The [plus] method creates a new list, copies all the people from [l] into it, and then [l] references this new list, while the old one is discarded by the garbage collector. The method [ajouter] adds the person to the existing list without copying them. Line 23 stores a second reference, [l3], to the list [l]; after the call to [l.ajouter(...)], both references still point to the same object (line 9 of the results), which proves that the list was not recreated. For a large list, or within a loop, the difference in performance is significant. The choice between the two styles is evident in JDK: the immutable objects [String] and [BigDecimal] return new objects; lists and [StringBuilder] are modified.

    4.4. No indexers: get and set methods

    Here, we continue to use the [ListeDePersonnes] class. If [l] is a [ListeDePersonnes] object, we want to be able to refer to the person at index i in the [l] list for both reading and writing. Some languages allow you to define an “indexer” for this purpose, which enables the [l[i]] notation to be used on an object. Java does not allow this: the [[i]] notation is reserved for arrays. By convention, we write methods [get(int i)] and [set(int i, valeur)], just as the JDK lists do:

    4.5. No Structures: Primitive Types and Records

    4.5.1. Value and Reference

    Other languages, such as C or C#, offer structures in addition to classes: types whose variables directly contain the data, rather than a reference to an object. Java does not have them. It distinguishes between two families of types:

    • the eight primitive types ([byte], [short], [int], [long], [float], [double], [char], [boolean]): a variable of a primitive type contains the value itself;
    • reference types: classes (including [String]), interfaces, arrays, records, etc. A variable of a reference type contains a reference to an object, such as [null].

    // primitive types and reference types: value copying, reference copying
void main() {
     // Two variables of a primitive type
    int age1 = 10;
    int age2 = age1;
    IO.println("age1=" + age1 + ", age2=" + age2);
     // age2 is modified
    age2 = 30;
     // Checking age1 and age2
    IO.println("age1=" + age1 + ", age2=" + age2);

     // an object op1
    CPersonne op1 = new CPersonne();
    op1.nom = "paul";
    op1.age = 10;
    IO.println("op1=CPersonne(" + op1.nom + "," + op1.age + ")");
     // an op2 object
    CPersonne op2 = op1;
    IO.println("op2=CPersonne(" + op2.nom + "," + op2.age + ")");
     // op2 is modified
    op2.nom = "nicole";
    op2.age = 30;
     // Verification of op1 and op2
    IO.println("op1=CPersonne(" + op1.nom + "," + op1.age + ")");
    IO.println("op2=CPersonne(" + op2.nom + "," + op2.age + ")");

     // an explicit copy of the object
    CPersonne op3 = new CPersonne();
    op3.nom = op1.nom;
    op3.age = op1.age;
    op3.age = 50;
    IO.println("op1=CPersonne(" + op1.nom + "," + op1.age + ")");
    IO.println("op3=CPersonne(" + op3.nom + "," + op3.age + ")");
}

// class CPersonne
class CPersonne {
    String nom = "";
    int age;
}

    The declaration [int age1 = 10;] (line 4) reserves a memory location that contains the integer 10: the value of [age1] is the integer itself. In the case of the class, the object ([nom], [age]) is created explicitly using the operator [new] (line 13). The object is placed in a memory area managed by the garbage collector, the heap, and the value of [op1] is the address (the reference) of this object.

    When [int age2 = age1;] is written in the program (line 5), the value of [age1]—the integer 10—is copied into [age2]: this is a value copy. Modifying [age2] does not modify [age1] (line 3 of the results). Now consider the instruction [CPersonne op2 = op1;] (line 18). The value of [op1] is copied to [op2], but since this value is the object’s address, the object itself is not duplicated: [op1] and [op2] refer to the same object. If the object pointed to by [op2] is modified, the object pointed to by [op1] is also modified since they are the same (lines 6–7 of the results). To obtain a second object, you must create it and copy the fields from the first one into it (lines 28–30): modifying the copy does not modify the original (lines 8–9 of the results).

    From these explanations, we can conclude that:

    • the value of a variable of a primitive type is the data itself;
    • the value of a reference-type variable is the address of the object it points to;
    • assignment and parameter passing always copy the value of the variable: the data itself for a primitive type, the reference for an object.

    Each primitive type corresponds to a so-called “wrapper” class in the [java.lang] package: [Integer] for [int], [Double] for [double], [Boolean] for [boolean], and so on. The compiler automatically converts a primitive value to a wrapper object and vice versa (“autoboxing” and “unboxing”): we’ll need this with generics, which only accept reference types. A variable [Integer] can be equal to [null], but a variable [int] never can.

    To represent a small composite piece of data (a point, a color, a date, an amount) that is treated as a value, Java uses immutable classes: their objects cannot be modified after they are created. Sharing a reference to an immutable object is safe: no one can modify it, and the object then behaves like a value. Two tools round out this system: the *[equals]* method, which compares two objects based on their content, and records, which declare an immutable class in a single line. This is the subject of the following two paragraphs.

    4.5.2. Equality of Two Objects: equals and hashCode

    As we have seen, the [==] operator applied to two references indicates whether they refer to the same object, and the [equals] method, inherited from [Object], does the same. For two distinct objects with the same content to be considered equal, a class must redefine the method [equals], and, necessarily along with it, the method [hashCode]. void main() {
    Personne p1 = new Personne("paul", 10);

     // == compares references; equals compares values
    IO.println("p1 == p2 : " + (p1 == p2) + ", p1.equals(p2) : " + p1.equals(p2)
            + ", p1.equals(p3) : " + p1.equals(p3));
     // Two equal objects have the same hash code
    IO.println("p1.hashCode() == p2.hashCode() : " + (p1.hashCode() == p2.hashCode()));
     // A set does not contain two equal objects
    Set<Personne> personnes = new HashSet<>();
    personnes.add(p1);
    personnes.add(p2);
    personnes.add(p3);
    IO.println("taille de l'ensemble : " + personnes.size());
    IO.println("l'ensemble contient (paul,10) : " + personnes.contains(new Personne("paul", 10)));
}

class Personne {
     // fields
    private final String nom;
    private final int age;

     // constructor
    public Personne(String nom, int age) {
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
    }

     // Two people are equal if they have the same name and age
    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
         // same object?
        if (this == o) {
            return true;
        }
         // Is o a Person (and not null)?
        if (!(o instanceof Personne autre)) {
            return false;
        }
         // field comparison
        return age == autre.age && Objects.equals(nom, autre.nom);
    }

     // Hash code consistent with `equals`
    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(nom, age);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Personne(" + nom + "," + age + ")";
    }
}
    • lines 32–44: The method [equals] overrides that of the class [Object]. Its parameter is of type [Object]: a person can be compared to any object. The method follows a standard pattern:
      • lines 35–37: an object is equal to itself;
      • lines 39–41: the expression [o instanceof Personne autre] (Java 16) is true if [o] refers to an object of type [Personne] (or a derived class), and false otherwise, in particular if [o] is equal to [null]. When it is true, the variable [autre], of type [Personne], refers to the object [o]: its fields can be used. This “type pattern” is explained in detail at the end of the chapter;
      • line 43: the fields are compared. The method [Objects.equals(a, b)] compares two objects with [equals] by handling the case where one of them is [null];
    • lines 47–50: The method [hashCode] returns an integer calculated from the same fields, in this case by the method [Objects.hash]. The rule is mandatory: two objects that are equal in the sense of [equals] must have the same hash code. The dictionaries and sets in JDK (next chapter) sort objects based on this code and would no longer function if the rule were not followed;
    • lines 12–17: A [HashSet] set never contains two equal objects: adding [p2], which is equal to [p1], has no effect, and the search for a new person ([paul, 10]) is successful.

    // Immutable objects: an immutable class and a record
void main() {
    Point a = new Point(1, 2);
     // a.x =   5; // rejected: the x field is final
    Point b = a.deplacer(3, 4);
    IO.println("a=" + a + ", b=" + b);

     // a record: constructor, accessors, toString, equals, and hashCode are generated
    Couleur rouge = new Couleur(255, 0, 0);
    Couleur rouge2 = new Couleur(255, 0, 0);
    IO.println("rouge=" + rouge + ", r=" + rouge.r());
    IO.println("rouge.equals(rouge2) : " + rouge.equals(rouge2) + ", rouge == rouge2 : " + (rouge == rouge2));
     // a modified copy, created by hand-written methods
    Couleur rose = rouge.avecV(128).avecB(128);
    IO.println("rouge=" + rouge + ", rose=" + rose);
}

// an immutable class: final, private and final fields, no modifiers
final class Point {
    private final int x;
    private final int y;

    public Point(int x, int y) {
        this.x = x;
        this.y = y;
    }

    public int getX() {
        return x;
    }

    public int getY() {
        return y;
    }

     // we don’t modify the point: we return a new one
    public Point deplacer(int dx, int dy) {
        return new Point(x + dx, y + dy);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "(" + x + "," + y + ")";
    }
}

// a record: an immutable class declared in a single line... or almost
record Couleur(int r, int v, int b) {
     // Methods that return a modified copy of the record
    public Couleur avecV(int v) {
        return new Couleur(r, v, b);
    }

    public Couleur avecB(int b) {
        return new Couleur(r, v, b);
    }
}
    • lines 19–45: a manually written immutable class. It is final, so that no derived class can add mutable state to it; its fields are private and [final]; it has no modifiers. To “move” a point, the method [deplacer] returns a new point (lines 37–39);
    • Line 48: a record (Java 16). The header [record Couleur(int r, int v, int b)] declares a final class with three private fields—[final], known as the record components—a three-parameter constructor, and three accessors: [r()], [v()], [b()], and methods [toString], [equals], and [hashCode], all of which use the components;
    • Lines 50–56: You can add methods to a record. Since a record is immutable, it cannot be modified: instead, a copy is created in which one component has been changed. These methods are called “withers” (from the English “with”); other languages provide an expression for this purpose, [with], which does not exist in Java 25;
    • line 11: An accessor for a component is named after the component, without the prefix [get];
    • line 12: two records of the same components are equal in the sense of [equals], even though they are distinct;
    • line 14: the “wither” methods are chained together.
