    4.6. Interfaces

    4.6.1. A First Example

    An interface is a set of method declarations that forms a contract. A class that chooses to implement an interface commits to providing an implementation of all the abstract methods defined in the interface. The compiler verifies this implementation.

    For example, here is the (simplified) definition of the [java.util.Iterator<E>] interface of JDK, which allows you to iterate over the elements of a collection: [public interface Iterator<E> { boolean hasNext(); E next(); }]. The methods of the interface are defined only by their signatures, followed by a semicolon: they have no code and are implicitly public and abstract. It is the classes that implement the interface that provide code for its methods. A class named [C] declares that it implements the interface using the keyword [implements]: [public class C implements Iterator<String>], and it must then define the two public methods [public boolean hasNext() { ... }] and [public String next() { ... }].

    A common convention (though not universal—JDK does not follow it) is to start an interface name with the letter I. The following examples make up the [Statistiques] folder. Consider the following interface, [IStats.java]:

    1
2
3
4
5
6
7
    public interface IStats {
     // average of a series of values
    double moyenne();

     // standard deviation of the series
    double ecartType();
}

    The [IStats] interface contains:

    • a method [moyenne]: to calculate the mean of a series of values;
    • a method [ecartType]: to calculate the standard deviation.

    Note that it is not specified anywhere which set of values is being referred to. It could be the average grades of a class, the monthly average sales of a particular product, the average temperature in a given location… This is the principle behind interfaces: we assume the existence of methods in the object but not that of specific data. The methods do not have the prefix [get]: they are calculations rather than field accesses, and this choice will allow a record to implement the interface.

    A first class implementing the [IStats] interface could be a class used to store the grades of students in a class for a given subject. A student is characterized by the following [Eleve] record, [Eleve.java]:

    import java.util.Arrays;

public class TableauDeNotes implements IStats {
     // fields
    private final String matiere;
    private final Note[] notes;
    private final double moyenne;
    private final double ecartType;

     // constructor
    public TableauDeNotes(String matiere, Note[] notes) {
         // data storage
        this.matiere = matiere;
        this.notes = notes;
         // calculation of the average of the grades
        double somme = 0;
        for (Note note : notes) {
            somme += note.valeur();
        }
        moyenne = notes.length != 0 ? somme / notes.length : -1;
         // calculating the standard deviation
        double carres = 0;
        for (Note note : notes) {
            carres += Math.pow(note.valeur() - moyenne, 2);
        }
        ecartType = notes.length != 0 ? Math.sqrt(carres / notes.length) : -1;
    }

     // accessors
    public String getMatiere() {
        return matiere;
    }

    public Note[] getNotes() {
        return notes;
    }

     // Implementation of interface methods IStats
    @Override
    public double moyenne() {
        return moyenne;
    }

    @Override
    public double ecartType() {
        return ecartType;
    }

     // toString
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "matière=" + matiere + ", notes=" + Arrays.toString(notes);
    }
}
    • Line 3: The class [TableauDeNotes] implements the interface [IStats]. It must therefore implement the methods [moyenne] and [ecartType]. These are implemented on lines 39–47. The annotation [@Override] is also used for implementing an interface method;
    • lines 5–8: four fields [final]: the subject for which the object stores grades, the grade array, the average, and the standard deviation of the grades;
    • lines 11–27: the constructor. Here, we assume that the grades passed to the constructor will not change afterward. Therefore, we use the constructor to immediately calculate the mean and standard deviation of these grades and store them. A field such as [final], like [moyenne], can be assigned a value in the constructor (line 20); it cannot be assigned a value afterward. The expressions [condition ? valeur1 : valeur2] set the mean and standard deviation of an empty array to -1. [Math.pow(x, 2)] calculates x², and [Math.sqrt] calculates the square root;
    • lines 50–53: the method [toString] uses the static method [Arrays.toString], which returns the elements of an array in square brackets, separated by commas, each converted to a string by its method [toString], in this case, the one for record [Note].

    import java.util.List;

public class ListeDeNotes implements IStats {
     // fields
    private final String matiere;
    private final List<Note> notes;
     // Stored mean and standard deviation (null: not yet calculated)
    private Double moyenne;
    private Double ecartType;

     // manufacturer
    public ListeDeNotes(String matiere, List<Note> notes) {
        this.matiere = matiere;
        this.notes = notes;
    }

     // accessories
    public String getMatiere() {
        return matiere;
    }

    public List<Note> getNotes() {
        return notes;
    }

     // Add a note
    public void ajouter(Note note) {
        notes.add(note);
         // The mean and standard deviation must be recalculated
        moyenne = null;
        ecartType = null;
    }

     // average of scores: calculated on the first request
    @Override
    public double moyenne() {
        if (moyenne == null) {
            moyenne = calculerMoyenne();
        }
        return moyenne;
    }

     // Standard deviation of scores: calculated on the first request
    @Override
    public double ecartType() {
        if (ecartType == null) {
            ecartType = calculerEcartType();
        }
        return ecartType;
    }

    private double calculerMoyenne() {
        if (notes.isEmpty()) {
            return -1;
        }
        double somme = 0;
        for (Note note : notes) {
            somme += note.valeur();
        }
        return somme / notes.size();
    }

    private double calculerEcartType() {
        if (notes.isEmpty()) {
            return -1;
        }
        double m = moyenne();
        double carres = 0;
        for (Note note : notes) {
            carres += Math.pow(note.valeur() - m, 2);
        }
        return Math.sqrt(carres / notes.size());
    }

     // toString
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "matière=" + matiere + ", notes=" + notes;
    }
}
    • line 3: the class [ListeDeNotes] implements the interface [IStats];
    • line 6: Notes are now stored in a list rather than an array;
    • lines 27–32: You can now add a grade to those already stored. The mean and standard deviation are no longer calculated in the constructor but on demand, within the interface methods themselves: [moyenne] (lines 35–41) and [ecartType] (lines 44–50). Once calculated, these values are stored so they are not recalculated with every request: they are said to be cached. Adding a score invalidates the cache;
    • lines 8–9: the cache. The type [Double] is the wrapper class for the primitive type [double]: unlike a [double] variable, a [Double] variable can have the value [null], which here means “not yet calculated.” Uninitialized fields are set to [null] when the object is constructed;
    • lines 38 and 40: the compiler automatically converts the [double] returned by [calculerMoyenne] into the object [Double] (“autoboxing”), and the object [Double] into [double] for the method’s return value (“unboxing”).

    };

    afficheStats(francais);

    francais.ajouter(new Note(new Eleve("Jérôme", "Jaric"), 10));
    afficheStats(francais);
     // A variable can have an interface as its type
    IStats stats = anglais;

    stats = francais;
    IO.println("Moyenne de français : " + stats.moyenne());

// Displaying the mean and standard deviation of an object that implements IStats
void afficheStats(IStats valeurs) {
    IO.println(valeurs + ", Moyenne=" + valeurs.moyenne() + ", Ecart-type=" + valeurs.ecartType());
}
    • lines 3–5: creation of an array of students;
    • line 6: creation of an array of grades;
    • line 8: a [TableauDeNotes] object whose mean and standard deviation are displayed on line 10;
    • line 12: an object [ListeDeNotes], whose mean and standard deviation are displayed on line 13. [List.of(notes)] returns a read-only list of the array’s elements; the constructor of the [ArrayList] class turns it into a modifiable list to which notes can be added;
    • line 15: a new note is added, followed by a refresh of the display;
    • Lines 25–27: The method *[afficheStats] takes a *[IStats] type as a parameter, which is an interface type. This means that the actual parameter can be any object that implements the *[IStats]* interface. When using a data object of an interface type, only the methods of the interface that are implemented by the data object are used. The rest are ignored. This property is similar to the polymorphism discussed for classes. If a set of classes Ci that are not related to one another through inheritance (and therefore cannot use inheritance-based polymorphism) share a set of methods with the same signature, it may be useful to group these methods into an interface I that all the relevant classes would implement. Instances of these classes Ci can then be used as actual parameters for methods that accept a formal parameter of type I—that is, methods that use only the methods of the Ci objects defined in the interface I, and not the specific fields and methods of the various Ci classes;
    • lines 18–21: A variable can be of the type of an interface. It can then refer to any object of a class that implements the interface. The compiler allows access only to the methods of the interface (and to those of the class [Object], such as [toString]).

    Finally, note that interfaces can be implemented multiple times; that is, one can write [public class ClasseDerivee extends ClasseDeBase implements I1, I2, ..., In], where the Ij are interfaces: a class inherits from only one class but can implement as many interfaces as it wishes. An interface can itself extend one or more other interfaces: [interface I3 extends I1, I2].

    4.6.2. Default, static, and private interface methods

    Since Java 8, an interface can provide a default implementation for some of its methods, declared with the keyword [default]. A class that implements the interface can then use this implementation or provide its own. This makes it possible, in particular, to add a method to an already published interface without requiring all classes that implement it to be modified: this is how the collections in the JDK have been expanded over successive versions. An interface can also contain static methods (Java 8) and private methods (Java 9). The program [Classes17.java] provides an example:

    // default (Java 8), static (Java 8), and private (Java 9) interface methods
void main() {
    IForme[] formes = { new Carre(2), new Cercle(1), IForme.carreUnite() };
    for (IForme forme : formes) {
        IO.println(forme.description());
    }
     // The default method is inherited by the Carre class
    Carre carre = new Carre(3);
    IO.println(carre.description());
}

interface IForme {
     // abstract method: to be implemented
    double surface();

     // Method with a default implementation
    default String description() {
        return getClass().getSimpleName() + " de surface " + formater(surface());
    }

     // static method: it is called using the interface name
    static IForme carreUnite() {
        return new Carre(1);
    }

     // private method: can only be used by methods of the interface
    private String formater(double valeur) {
        return String.format("%.2f", valeur);
    }
}

// Carre uses the default implementation of description
// (static class because the interface creates squares: see Classes10)
static class Carre implements IForme {
    private final double cote;

    public Carre(double cote) {
        this.cote = cote;
    }

    @Override
    public double surface() {
        return cote * cote;
    }
}

// Circle provides its own description implementation
class Cercle implements IForme {
    private final double rayon;

    public Cercle(double rayon) {
        this.rayon = rayon;
    }

    @Override
    public double surface() {
        return Math.PI * rayon * rayon;
    }

    @Override
    public String description() {
        return String.format("Cercle de rayon %s et de surface %.2f", rayon, surface());
    }
}
    • lines 12–30: the [IForme] interface:
      • line 14: an abstract method [surface], to be implemented;
      • lines 17–19: a method [description] with a default implementation. This method can use the other methods of the interface ([surface], [formater]) and those of [Object] ([getClass]);
      • lines 22–24: a static method, which is called using the interface name: [IForme.carreUnite()] (line 3). This is a static factory method;
      • lines 27–29: a private method, accessible only to the methods of the interface. [String.format("%.2f", valeur)] formats the number to two decimal places, following the conventions of the system’s locale—in this case, the French decimal point;
    • lines 34–45: the class [Carre] implements only [surface]; it uses the method [description] by default. It is declared as [static] because the static method [carreUnite] of the interface creates squares (see [Classes10.java]);
    • lines 48–64: The class [Cercle] provides its own method, [description]. The format [%s] inserts the radius converted to a string by [Double.toString] (“1.0”), and the format [%.2f] inserts the area with two decimal places;
    • Line 9: The default method is inherited by the [Carre] class just like any other method: it can be called on a variable of type [Carre].

    A class can implement two interfaces, each of which provides a default method with the same signature: the compiler then requires the class to redefine the method, even if it means calling one of the two versions via [I1.super.methode()]. Unlike an abstract class, an interface has no state: it cannot declare instance fields, only constants ([static final], implicitly).

    4.7. Abstract classes

    public abstract class Utilisateur {
     // fields
    private final String login;
    private final String motDePasse;
    private final String role;

     // constructor
    @SuppressWarnings("this-escape")
    protected Utilisateur(String login, String motDePasse) throws ExceptionUtilisateurInconnu {
         // The information is saved
        this.login = login;
        this.motDePasse = motDePasse;
         // The user is identified
        String role = identifie();
         // Identified?
        if (role == null) {
            throw new ExceptionUtilisateurInconnu("[" + login + "," + motDePasse + "]");
        }
        this.role = role;
    }

     // toString
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Utilisateur[" + login + "," + motDePasse + "," + role + "]";
    }

     // Identification: returns the user's role or null if the user is not recognized
    protected abstract String identifie();
}
    • line 1: the class is declared abstract using the keyword [abstract];
    • Lines 9–20: the constructor for the class [Utilisateur]. This class stores information about a web application’s user. The application has various types of users authenticated by a username and password (lines 3–4). These two pieces of information are verified against a directory (LDAP) for some users, against a database for others, and so on. The constructor is [protected]: it is intended for the constructors of derived classes;
    • lines 11–12: the authentication information is stored;
    • line 14: they are verified by a method [identifie]. Because the identification method is not known at this level, it is declared abstract (line 29) with the keyword [abstract]. An abstract method has no body: derived classes will provide one. A class that has an abstract method must itself be declared abstract. The method [identifie] returns a string specifying the user’s role (basically, what they are authorized to do), or [null] if the user is not recognized;
    • lines 16–18: if the user is not recognized, an exception is thrown. The [ExceptionUtilisateurInconnu] exception is a checked exception (see below): the constructor must declare it using the [throws ExceptionUtilisateurInconnu] clause (line 9);
    • lines 23–26: the method [toString], which identifies an instance of the class.

    Here, we assume that the developer wants to control the creation of instances of the class [Utilisateur] and its derived classes, perhaps because they want to ensure that an exception of a certain type is thrown if the user is not recognized. Derived classes can rely on this constructor. To do so, they must provide the [identifie] method. Note that the constructor here calls a method overridden by the derived classes even though those classes have not yet executed their own constructors: the [identifie] method must therefore not use any fields of the derived class, as they have not yet been initialized. This is a practice that should be used with caution, and the compiler flags it when compiling with the [-Xlint:all] option, which enables all warnings (here without the annotation on line 8, hence the line number 13 in the message):

    1
2
3
4
5
    > javac -Xlint:all -d classes *.java
Utilisateur.java:13: warning: [this-escape] possible 'this' escape before subclass is fully initialized
        String role = identifie();
                               ^
1 warning

    The warning [this-escape] (Java 21) indicates that the object being constructed ([this]) “escapes” the constructor before being fully initialized. In this case, this is intentional and harmless, since the [identifie] methods of the derived classes do not use any fields. After verifying this, the warning is suppressed—for this constructor only—using the annotation [@SuppressWarnings("this-escape")] (line 8). The source code launcher ([java Main.java]) does not enable these warnings: it is a good idea to compile your programs regularly with [javac -Xlint:all], which is what we have done for all the programs in this course.

    public class ExceptionUtilisateurInconnu extends Exception {
     // class version number (see explanations)
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

    public ExceptionUtilisateurInconnu(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}
    • Line 1: It derives from the class [Exception]. It is therefore a checked exception: the compiler verifies that any method that can throw it declares it using a [throws] clause, and that any code that calls such a method either catches it or declares it in turn. An exception derived from [RuntimeException], such as [IllegalArgumentException], is not a checked exception;
    • line 3: Exceptions are “serializable” objects (convertible to a sequence of bytes); the compiler, with the [-Xlint:all] option, requires that a serializable class declare a version number [serialVersionUID]. We simply use the value 1;
    • Lines 5–7: It has only a single constructor that takes an error message as a parameter. This is passed to the parent class, which has the same constructor.

    An abstract class is similar to an interface: both declare methods that other classes must implement. However, an abstract class can have fields, constructors, and code common to its derived classes; conversely, a class can derive from only one abstract class, whereas it can implement multiple interfaces. The two are often combined: an interface defines the contract, and an abstract class that implements it factors out the code common to multiple implementations. This is what the example application in this chapter will do.

    4.8. Generic Classes, Interfaces, and Methods

    4.8.1. Generic Classes and Methods

    Suppose we want to write a class [PaireEntiers] that stores two integers and can swap them: two fields, [int premier] and [int second], and a method, [echanger()], that swaps their values using a temporary variable, [int temp]. If we then wanted a pair of strings, followed by a pair of people, we would write two more classes, [PaireChaines] and [PairePersonnes], identical to the previous one except for the type: [String] or [Personne] instead of [int].

    Generic classes, interfaces, and methods address the need for code that differs only in the type of certain data. They were introduced with Java 5 (2004): prior to that, the type [Object] was used, which accepted anything, at the cost of explicit type conversions and errors detected only at runtime. Note that Java does not support passing parameters by reference: a method cannot swap the values of two variables from the caller, but it can swap two elements of an object, a pair, or an array.

    // generic classes and methods
void main() {
     // --- a generic class Pair<T>
     // Integer
    Paire<Integer> pi = new Paire<>(1, 2);
    pi.echanger();
    IO.println("pi=" + pi);
     // String
    Paire<String> ps = new Paire<>("s1", "s2");
    ps.echanger();
    IO.println("ps=" + ps);
     // Person
    Personne p1 = new Personne("jean", "clu", 20), p2 = new Personne("pauline", "dard", 55);
    Paire<Personne> pp = new Paire<>(p1, p2);
    pp.echanger();
    IO.println("pp=" + pp);
     // The first element is of type Person: no conversion
    Personne premiere = pp.getPremier();
    IO.println("premier élément : " + premiere);

     // --- a generic method Generic2.echanger<T>
    Integer[] entiers = { 1, 2, 3 };
    Generic2.<Integer>echanger(entiers, 0, 2);
    IO.println("entiers=" + Arrays.toString(entiers));
     // the compiler infers T from the type of the actual parameters
    Personne[] personnes = { p1, p2 };
    Generic2.echanger(personnes, 0, 1);
    IO.println("personnes=" + Arrays.toString(personnes));

     // --- a generic class with a state: a stack of elements of type T
    Pile<Personne> pile = new Pile<>();
    pile.empiler(p1);
    pile.empiler(p2);
    IO.println("La pile contient " + pile.size() + " personnes");
    Personne sommet = pile.depiler();
    IO.println("Personne dépilée : " + sommet + ", il en reste " + pile.size());
     // pile.empiler("x  "); // rejected: the stack only accepts Person objects
}

// a generic class: a pair of two elements of type T
class Paire<T> {
    private T premier;
    private T second;

    public Paire(T premier, T second) {
        this.premier = premier;
        this.second = second;
    }

    public T getPremier() {
        return premier;
    }

    public T getSecond() {
        return second;
    }

     // we swap the two elements
    public void echanger() {
        T temp = premier;
        premier = second;
        second = temp;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "(" + premier + "," + second + ")";
    }
}

// a non-generic class with a generic method
class Generic2 {
     // swaps elements i and j of an array of type T
    public static <T> void echanger(T[] tableau, int i, int j) {
        T temp = tableau[i];
        tableau[i] = tableau[j];
        tableau[j] = temp;
    }
}

// a stack of elements of type T
class Pile<T> {
     // the elements of the stack
    private final List<T> elements = new ArrayList<>();

     // number of elements
    public int size() {
        return elements.size();
    }

     // add an element to the top of the stack
    public void empiler(T element) {
        elements.add(element);
    }

     // removing the element at the top of the stack
    public T depiler() {
        if (elements.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("pile vide");
        }
        return elements.removeLast();
    }
}

// a person
record Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age) {
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]";
    }
}
    • lines 41–69: The class *[Paire] is parameterized by a type denoted as *[T], enclosed in angle brackets after the class name. You can name it whatever you like; by convention, it is an uppercase letter ([T] for type, [E] for element, [K] and [V] for key and value). This type, [T], is then used in the class just like any other type: for the two fields, the constructor parameters, the results of the accessors, and the temporary variable [temp] (line 60). The class [Paire] is said to be a generic class;
    • Line 5: When using a generic class parameterized by the types T1, T2, …, these types must be specified. Here, [Paire<Integer>] is a pair of [Integer] objects. A generic parameter can only be a reference type: we write [Paire<Integer>], not [Paire<int>]. The integers 1 and 2 are automatically converted to [Integer] objects (“autoboxing”). On the right, the “diamond” operator [new Paire<>(...)] allows the compiler to infer the type [Integer] from that of the variable. Lines 9 and 14: the same applies to the types [String] and [Personne];
    • Line 18: The method [getPremier] of a [Paire<Personne>] returns an object of type [Personne], without conversion;
    • lines 72–79: the class [Generic2] is not generic, but its static method [echanger] is: the parameter of type [<T>] is declared before the return type (line 74). The method swaps elements i and j of an array of elements of type [T];
    • line 23: the method *[echanger] is called, specifying the type *[T] between ***[<>]*. In fact, the compiler is able to infer [T] from the type of the actual parameters. Therefore, the notation in line 27 is valid, and this is the one used in practice;
    • lines 82–103: a generic class with a state: a stack of elements of type [T]. Elements are pushed onto the top of the stack and popped from the top. The elements are stored in a generic list of type [List<T>] (line 84), which is itself parameterized by the [T] type of the stack. The method [removeLast] (Java 21) retrieves and returns the last element of the list. An empty stack throws a [IllegalStateException] exception, the exception defined by Java for an operation requested from an object that is not in the expected state;
    • line 31: a stack of people. The compiler guarantees that it will contain only people: the statement on line 37 would be rejected. The method [depiler] returns an object of type [Personne], without conversion;
    • lines 106–111: The person is a record for which the method [toString] has been redefined.

    4.8.2. Generic parameter bounds

    In the [Paire<T>] class, the compiler knows nothing about the [T] type: it allows only the methods of the [Object] class to be called on objects of type [T]. To be able to use other methods, we constrain the generic parameter with the keyword [extends]:

    Constraint
    Meaning
    [<T extends Classe>]
    T must be the specified class or a derived class
    [<T extends Interface>]
    T must implement the specified interface (written as [extends], not [implements])
    [<T extends Classe & I1 & I2>]
    Multiple parameters: at most one class, listed first, followed by interfaces
    [<T extends Comparable<T>>]
    A bound that uses T itself: T must be comparable to T

    There is no constraint requiring that T be a reference type (it always is) or that it have a parameterless constructor: you cannot write [new T()] in a generic class (see type erasure below). The program [Classes19.java] uses a constraint:

    // the bounds of generic parameters
void main() {
     // --- T is always an object type: int is replaced by Integer
    Paire<Integer> pi = new Paire<>(1, 2);
     // Pair<int> pe = new Pair<>(1, 2)  ; // error: int is a primitive type
    IO.println("pi=" + pi);

     // --- the bound T extends IValeur
     // sort pairs of objects of type Random
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        Paire<Aleatoire> paire = new Paire<>(new Aleatoire(), new Aleatoire());
        IO.print("Avant --> " + paire);
        Generic4.ordonner(paire);
        IO.println("   Après --> " + paire);
    }
     // Sort a pair of objects of type String
    Paire<Chaine> chaines = new Paire<>(new Chaine("xxxxxxxxxxxxxx"), new Chaine("xx"));
    IO.println("Avant --> " + chaines);
    Generic4.ordonner(chaines);
    IO.println("Après --> " + chaines);
     // Generic4.ordonner(p  i); // error: Integer does not implement IValeur
}

// a pair of two elements of type T
class Paire<T> {
    private T premier;
    private T second;

    public Paire(T premier, T second) {
        this.premier = premier;
        this.second = second;
    }

    public T getPremier() {
        return premier;
    }

    public T getSecond() {
        return second;
    }

    public void echanger() {
        T temp = premier;
        premier = second;
        second = temp;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "(" + premier + "," + second + ")";
    }
}

// type T must implement IValeur
class Generic4 {
    public static <T extends IValeur> void ordonner(Paire<T> paire) {
         // if the first element is greater than the second, swap the elements
        if (paire.getPremier().valeur() > paire.getSecond().valeur()) {
            paire.echanger();
        }
    }
}

// an object with an integer value
interface IValeur {
    int valeur();
}

// an object with a random value
class Aleatoire implements IValeur {
     // a random number generator shared by all instances
     // (initialized with a fixed seed so that results are reproducible)
    private static final Random generateur = new Random(2026);
     // value of the object
    private final int valeur = generateur.nextInt(100);

    @Override
    public int valeur() {
        return valeur;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return String.valueOf(valeur);
    }
}

// an object whose value is the length of a string
class Chaine implements IValeur {
    private final String s;

    public Chaine(String s) {
        this.s = s;
    }

    @Override
    public int valeur() {
        return s.length();
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return s;
    }
}
    • line 5: if you uncomment this line, the compiler reports an error because the type *[int]* is a primitive type;
    • Lines 55–62: The generic method [ordonner] requires that the type [T] implement the interface [IValeur] (lines 65–67). This interface has a method named [valeur], used on line 58, which returns the value of the object of type [T]. Without the bound, the compiler would reject the call to [paire.getPremier().valeur()]: any [T] type does not have a [valeur] method. The two elements of the pair are swapped only if the value of the first is greater than that of the second: the method [ordonner] sorts the two elements in ascending order by value;
    • lines 70–86: The class [Aleatoire] implements the interface [IValeur]. The value of an instance is a random number between 0 and 99 (line 75), provided by a random number generator in the [Random] class shared by all instances (line 73). This generator is initialized with a fixed “seed”: it therefore always produces the same sequence of numbers, making the results reproducible. If reproducibility is not required, the generator created by [new Random()] is used; for security purposes, the class [SecureRandom] is used instead;
    • lines 89–105: The class [Chaine] also implements the interface [IValeur]: the value of an instance is the length of the character string passed to the constructor;
    • lines 10–15: Pairs of objects of type [Aleatoire] are ordered;
    • lines 17–20: a pair of objects of type [Chaine] is ordered;
    • line 21: if this line is uncommented, the compiler reports that the type [Integer] does not satisfy the bound.

    4.8.3. Generic Interfaces: Comparable<T> and Comparator<T>

    To illustrate the concept of a generic interface, we will sort an array of people according to different criteria. The method that allows us to sort an array is the static method [sort] of the class [java.util.Arrays]. It is overloaded; we will use two variants:

    • [Arrays.sort(Object[] tableau)] sorts the array according to the natural order of its elements: these elements must implement the [Comparable<T>] interface, whose sole method, [int compareTo(T autre)], compares the current object to the [autre] object;
    • [Arrays.sort(T[] tableau, Comparator<? super T> comparateur)] sorts the array according to the order defined by a comparator object, which implements the [Comparator<T>] interface, whose [int compare(T x, T y)] method compares two objects (the type [? super T] is explained in the following paragraph).

    The methods [compareTo] and [compare] follow the same rule: they return a positive number if x > y, 0 if x == y, and a negative number if x < y. It is up to the developer to define the meaning of the operators <, ==, and >. For example, if [p1] and [p2] are two [Personne] objects, we can say that p1 > p2 if the name of [p1] comes after the name of [p2] in alphabetical order. This will result in an ascending sort based on the people’s names. If we want to sort by age, we’ll say that p1 > p2 if the age of [p1] is greater than the age of [p2]. To sort in descending order, simply reverse the signs of the results.

     // display
    affiche("Tableau à trier", personnes);
     // sort by natural order of individuals (Comparable): age
    Arrays.sort(personnes);
    affiche("Tableau après le tri selon l'âge", personnes);
     // sort by last name and first name (Comparator)
    Arrays.sort(personnes, new CompareNoms());
    affiche("Tableau après le tri selon les nom et prénom", personnes);
     // sort by age in descending order, with an anonymous class
    Arrays.sort(personnes, new Comparator<Personne>() {
        @Override
        public int compare(Personne p1, Personne p2) {
            return Integer.compare(p2.getAge(), p1.getAge());
        }
    });
    affiche("Tableau après le tri selon l'âge décroissant", personnes);
}

// display of a table of people
void affiche(String texte, Personne[] personnes) {
    IO.println(texte + "-".repeat(50 - texte.length()));
    for (Personne p : personnes) {
        IO.println(p);
    }
}

// one person, comparable to another person
class Personne implements Comparable<Personne> {
    private final String prenom;
    private final String nom;
    private final int age;

    public Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age) {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public String getPrenom() {
        return prenom;
    }

    public String getNom() {
        return nom;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

     // The natural order of people: sorted by age
    @Override
    public int compareTo(Personne autre) {
        return Integer.compare(age, autre.age);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]";
    }
}

// comparison of the first and last names of two people
class CompareNoms implements Comparator<Personne> {
     // comparison of strings according to the rules of the French language
    private final Collator collator = Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRENCH);

    @Override
    public int compare(Personne p1, Personne p2) {
         // comparing first names
        int i = collator.compare(p1.getNom(), p2.getNom());
        if (i != 0) {
            return i;
        }
         // Surname equality: comparing first names
        return collator.compare(p1.getPrenom(), p2.getPrenom());
    }
}
    • lines 3–7: the array of people;
    • lines 35–68: the class [Personne] implements the generic interface [Comparable<Personne>]: its objects are comparable to other people. Its method [compareTo] (lines 59–62) defines the natural order of people, in this case by age. The static method [Integer.compare(a, b)] returns a negative, zero, or positive number depending on whether [a] is less than, equal to, or greater than [b]: this is exactly what the method [compareTo] expects;
    • line 11: sorting in natural order;
    • line 14: sorts the array of people by last name and first name. The second parameter of the [sort] method is an instance of the [CompareNoms] class, which implements the generic interface [Comparator<Personne>];
    • lines 71–85: the class [CompareNoms]. Its method [compare] implements the method [int compare(T x, T y)] of the interface [Comparator<T>], where [T] = [Personne]. Strings are not compared using their [compareTo] method, which follows the order of character codes (uppercase letters before lowercase, accented letters after “z”), but rather by a [Collator] object (line 73) that applies the sorting rules for the French language;
    • lines 17–22: sorting by age in descending order. The comparator this time is an instance of an anonymous class: the expression [new Comparator<Personne>() { ... }] declares an unnamed class that implements the [Comparator<Personne>] interface and immediately creates an instance of that class. The body of the class (lines 18–21) provides the method [compare]. An anonymous class avoids having to declare a class that is used only once;
    • line 28: the [repeat] method (Java 11) pads a string: the title line is padded with dashes up to 50 characters.

    We have now encountered three types of classes declared inside another: static nested classes ([static class]), inner classes (such as [static], which are associated with an object of the enclosing class), and anonymous classes. In Chapter 7, we’ll see that for an interface with only one abstract method, such as [Comparator], we can use an even shorter alternative than an anonymous class: a lambda, [Arrays.sort(personnes, (p1, p2) -> Integer.compare(p2.getAge(), p1.getAge()));], or a method reference, [Arrays.sort(personnes, Comparator.comparing(Personne::getNom));].

    4.8.4. Wildcards and Type Erasure

    A [List<Integer>] is not a [List<Number>], even though [Integer] derives from [Number]: if it were, we could add a [Double] to a list of integers via a variable of type [List<Number>]. A method that accepts a [List<Number>] therefore rejects a [List<Integer>]. To write methods that accept lists of elements of related types, Java uses wildcards:

    Type
    Meaning
    Usage
    [List<? extends Number>]
    a list of elements of an unknown type derived from [Number]
    You can read [Number] from it, but you cannot add elements to it
    [List<? super Integer>]
    A list of items of an unknown type from which [Integer] is derived ([Integer], [Number], [Object])
    [Integer] can be added to this list
    [List<?>]
    a list of items of an unknown type
    You can read [Object]

    The program [Classes21.java] illustrates wildcards and a special feature of Java generics: type erasure:

    // wildcards, bounds, and type erasure
void main() {
    List<Integer> entiers = List.of(1, 2, 3);
    List<Double> reels = List.of(1.5, 2.25);
     // ? extends Number: a list of elements of a type derived from Number
    IO.println("Somme d'entiers : " + somme(entiers));
    IO.println("Somme de réels : " + somme(reels));
     // ? super Integer: a list that can hold Integers
    List<Number> nombres = new ArrayList<>();
    ajouterEntiers(nombres, 3);
    nombres.add(2.5);
    IO.println("nombres=" + nombres + ", somme=" + somme(nombres));
     // a recursive bound: T must be comparable to itself
    IO.println("max : " + max(List.of("paul", "jean", "valentine")) + ", " + max(entiers));
     // type erasure: at runtime, a list is a list
    List<String> l1 = new ArrayList<>();
    List<Integer> l2 = new ArrayList<>();
    IO.println("même classe : " + (l1.getClass() == l2.getClass()) + " (" + l1.getClass().getName() + ")");
}

// sum of the elements in a list of numbers
double somme(List<? extends Number> valeurs) {
    double somme = 0;
    for (Number valeur : valeurs) {
        somme += valeur.doubleValue();
    }
     // valeurs.add(  1); // rejected: the exact type of the elements is unknown
    return somme;
}

// adding the integers 1, 2, ..., n to a list capable of holding Integers
void ajouterEntiers(List<? super Integer> liste, int n) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        liste.add(i);
    }
}

// the largest element in a non-empty list
<T extends Comparable<? super T>> T max(List<T> elements) {
    T max = elements.getFirst();
    for (T element : elements) {
        if (element.compareTo(max) > 0) {
            max = element;
        }
    }
    return max;
}
    • Lines 22–29: The [somme] method accepts a list of elements of any type derived from [Number]: [Integer], [Double], [BigDecimal]… It treats the elements as [Number] and uses their [doubleValue] method. Java does not support generic arithmetic: you cannot write [a + b] for two objects of type [T], hence the need to use [double]. Adding an element to the list (line 27) is rejected: the compiler does not know whether it is a list of [Integer] or [Double];
    • lines 6–7: the same method concatenates a list of [Integer] with a list of [Double]. [List.of(...)] creates a read-only list;
    • lines 32–36: the [ajouterEntiers] method accepts any list capable of holding [Integer] entries, in this case a [List<Number>] (line 10). We follow the rule “producer: [extends], consumer: [super]”: a list whose elements are read is written using [extends], and a list that is filled is written using [super];
    • Lines 39–47: The generic method *[max] returns the largest element in a list. The [T extends Comparable<? super T>] bound requires that the elements be comparable to one another; it applies to strings as well as integers (line 14). The [getFirst]* method (Java 21) returns the first element of the list;
    • lines 16–18: At runtime, a ***[List<String>] and a ***[List<Integer>] are two objects of the same class, *[ArrayList]*. The compiler checks the generic types and then erases them: the compiled code only recognizes [ArrayList] and [Object], and conversions are inserted where necessary. This “type erasure,” adopted in 2004 to ensure that generic code remains compatible with existing code, explains several limitations: you cannot write [new T()] or [new T[10]], nor can you test [o instanceof List<String>], nor can you use a primitive type as a generic parameter.

    Unlike other languages such as C#, where interfaces can declare abstract static members to implement generic computations, Java does not allow requiring a type like [T] to have a static method: static methods of an interface are called using the interface’s name and are not inherited by the classes that implement it.

    4.9. Packages

    To write a line on the screen, we use the [IO.println(...)] statement. If we look at the definition of the [IO] class in the JDK documentation, we find that it is part of the [java.lang] package. This means that its full name is [java.lang.IO] and that we could write [java.lang.IO.println(...)]. The classes in the [java.lang] package ([String], [Object], [Math], [Integer]…) are always referred to by their simple names. For the others, a [import] clause is used, placed at the beginning of the file:

    • [import java.util.List;] imports the class [List] from the package [java.util];
    • [import java.util.*;] imports all public classes from the [java.util] package on demand;
    • [import module java.base;] (Java 25) imports all public classes from the packages exported by the [java.base] module (see below). This is what a compact file does implicitly;
    • [import static java.lang.Math.sqrt;] imports a static member of a class, which can then be used without specifying the class name: [sqrt(2)].

    When the compiler encounters a class’s short name, it looks for it in the current package and among the imported classes. A [import] clause adds nothing to the program: it merely avoids having to write out the full names.

    When you create a class, you place it in a package. The purpose of packages is to avoid name conflicts between classes, for example, when they are distributed. Consider two companies, E1 and E2, distributing classes packaged in the archives [e1.jar] and [e2.jar], respectively. Suppose a customer C purchases these two sets of classes, in which both companies have defined a class named [Personne]. If company E1 creates its classes in a package named [e1] and company E2 creates its classes in a package named [e2], the two classes [Personne] will then be named [e1.Personne] and [e2.Personne]. The client can import one of them and refer to the other by its full name. The package resolves this ambiguity. By convention, package names are in lowercase and begin with the reverse domain name of the organization that publishes them ([com.mysql.cj.jdbc], [org.hibernate]…); for our examples, we will use short names.

    To place a class in a package, you write the declaration [package nom;] at the top of its file. Unlike other languages, Java requires a one-to-one correspondence between packages and directories: the source files for the [e1] package are stored in a folder named [e1], and those for the [impots.dao] package are stored in a folder named [impots/dao], starting from the root of the source directory.     4.9.1. Modules

    Starting with Java 9, packages are themselves grouped into modules (“Java Platform Module System,” JPMS). JDK is divided into modules: [java.base] contains the core packages ([java.lang], [java.util], [java.math], [java.io]…), [java.sql] provides database access, [java.net.http] is the client, HTTP, etc. A module declares, in a file named [module-info.java] located at the root of its source code, its name, the modules it requires ([requires java.sql;]), and the packages it makes available to other modules ([exports impots.metier;]): An unexported package is invisible from the outside, even for its public classes. The classes in an application that does not declare a module—such as ours—belong to the unnamed module (line 5 of the results), which has access to all modules. This is the case for most applications, and for all those in this course: modules are primarily of interest to library authors and to the JDK module itself.

    4.10. Records

    Many classes serve only to carry data: a person, a grade, a tax bracket… For these, we always write the same code: private fields and [final], a constructor that copies its parameters into the fields, accessors, a [toString] method that displays the fields, and the [equals] and [hashCode] methods. Java 16 introduced records: the compiler generates this code from a single-line declaration. We encountered them in the section on immutable objects; the program [Classes22.java] demonstrates them more fully:

    // records (Java 16)
void main() {
    Personne r1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    Personne r2 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
     // toString generated by the compiler
    IO.println(r1);
     // The accessors are named after the components
    IO.println("prénom=" + r1.prenom() + ", identité=" + r1.identite());
     // Equality by value: r1 and r2 are two different but equal objects
    IO.println("r1.equals(r2) : " + r1.equals(r2) + ", r1 == r2 : " + (r1 == r2));
     // The components are read-only
     // r1.age =   31; // rejected: the age field is final
     // a modified copy, using the “wither” method
    Personne r3 = r1.avecAge(31);
    IO.println(r3);
    IO.println("r1.equals(r3) : " + r1.equals(r3));
     // deconstruction into variables using a record pattern (Java 21)
    if (r1 instanceof Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age)) {
        IO.println("prénom=" + prenom + ", nom=" + nom + ", âge=" + age);
    }

     // the same thing using a class
    PersonneC c1 = new PersonneC("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    PersonneC c2 = new PersonneC("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    IO.println(c1);
    IO.println("c1.equals(c2) : " + c1.equals(c2));

     // two records that implement the same interface
    Enseignant e = new Enseignant("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61);
    IO.println(e);
    IO.println(e.identite());
     // Equality takes type into account: a Person is not equal to a Teacher
    Personne pe = new Personne("Lucile", "Dumas", 56);
    IO.println("pe.equals(e) : " + pe.equals(e));
     // the common type: the interface AvecIdentite
    AvecIdentite[] identites = { pe, e };
    for (AvecIdentite i : identites) {
        IO.println(i.identite());
    }
}

// an interface implemented by the records
interface AvecIdentite {
    String identite();
}

// A record: first_name, last_name, and age are its components
record Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age) implements AvecIdentite {
     // Methods can be added
    @Override
    public String identite() {
        return "[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]";
    }

     // a “wither” method: a copy in which one component has changed
    public Personne avecAge(int age) {
        return new Personne(prenom, nom, age);
    }
}

// A record cannot be derived from another record
record Enseignant(String prenom, String nom, int age, int section) implements AvecIdentite {
    @Override
    public String identite() {
        return "Enseignant[[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]," + section + "]";
    }
}

// A class is equivalent... or almost
final class PersonneC {
    private final String prenom;
    private final String nom;
    private final int age;

    public PersonneC(String prenom, String nom, int age) {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public String prenom() {
        return prenom;
    }

    public String nom() {
        return nom;
    }

    public int age() {
        return age;
    }
}
    • lines 48–59: the record [Personne]. The declaration [record Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age)] generates:
      • three private fields—[final], [prenom], [nom], and [age]—which are the components of the record;
      • a three-parameter constructor, known as the canonical constructor;
      • three public accessors: [prenom()], [nom()], and [age()] (line 8);
      • a method [toString] that displays the type name and its components (line 6);
      • the methods [equals] and [hashCode], which compare the values of the components rather than the references;
    • lines 51–53 and 56–58: a record, like a class, can have additional methods and implement interfaces (line 48);
    • line 10: [r1] and [r2] are two distinct objects ([==] is the same as [false]) but they are equal to [equals] because their components have the same values. For an ordinary class, [equals] compares references (line 26);
    • line 14: since a record is immutable, it cannot be modified (line 12): the “wither” method [avecAge] creates a copy of [r1] whose age has changed;
    • lines 18–20: a record pattern (Java 21): if [r1] is a [Personne], its components are extracted into the variables [prenom], [nom], and [age]. This is referred to as record decomposition. We will encounter these patterns again when filtering by pattern;
    • lines 62–67: a record is implicitly final and implicitly derives from the class [java.lang.Record]; it cannot derive from another class or record, nor can it be derived from. To give the records [Personne] and [Enseignant] a common type, we have them implement the same interface, in this case [AvecIdentite] (lines 43–45). The record [Enseignant] therefore contains the person’s components;
    • line 34: record equality takes into account the actual type of the objects: a [Personne] is never equal to a [Enseignant], even if their common components are equal;
    • lines 36–39: the common interface allows both records to be handled polymorphically;
    • lines 70–92: a class that resembles the [Personne] record… except that the fields, constructor, and accessors had to be written, and equality by value and [toString] are not provided.

    Let’s summarize the differences between a class and a record:

     
    Class
    Record
    Equality between [equals]
    same object (unless redefined)
    same component values, same type
    [toString]
    class name and hash code
    record name and components
    fields, constructor, accessors
    to be written
    generated by the declaration
    status
    editable or not
    immutable (fields [final]), no other instance fields
    modified copy
    to be written
    to be written (using "wither" methods)
    inheritance
    from a class, from multiple interfaces
    from no classes, from multiple interfaces; a record is always final

    A record is used for data defined by its value (a person retrieved from a database, a message exchanged over a network, a tax bracket), and a class is used for an object with an identity and behavior (a computing service, a connection, a mutable list). Note: A record is “superficially” immutable: if a component references a mutable object—such as a list—the contents of that list remain mutable. In such cases, immutable lists are used ([List.copyOf]).

    4.11. Record constructors

    The canonical constructor for a record simply copies its parameters into the fields. However, you may want to validate or normalize these parameters. Java provides the compact constructor for this purpose, as well as the ability to add other constructors. The program [Classes23.java] illustrates this:

    // Record constructors: compact constructor, other constructors
void main() {
    Personne p = new Personne("  Jean ", "Dupont", 30);
    IO.println(p.identite());
     // A record is immutable: aging creates a new person
    Personne p2 = p.vieillir();
    IO.println(p.identite() + " -> " + p2.identite());
     // another constructor
    Personne inconnu = new Personne("Martin");
    IO.println(inconnu.identite());
     // Validation checks for the compact constructor
    try {
        new Personne("Paul", " ", 20);
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        IO.println(ex.getMessage());
    }
    try {
        new Personne("Paul", "Martin", -4);
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        IO.println(ex.getMessage());
    }
     // A record with a method and a static factory
    Point pt = new Point(3, 4);
    IO.println("pt=" + pt + ", distance à l'origine : " + pt.distance() + ", origine=" + Point.origine());
}

record Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age) {
     // compact constructor: it validates and normalizes the parameters,
     // the fields are then initialized automatically
    Personne {
        prenom = verifier(prenom, "prénom");
        nom = verifier(nom, "nom");
        if (age < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("âge (" + age + ") invalide");
        }
    }

     // any other constructor must call the canonical constructor
    Personne(String nom) {
        this("?", nom, 0);
    }

     // a method that returns a new person
    public Personne vieillir() {
        return new Personne(prenom, nom, age + 1);
    }

    public String identite() {
        return "[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]";
    }

     // a static validation method
    private static String verifier(String valeur, String libelle) {
        if (valeur == null || valeur.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(libelle + " (" + valeur + ") invalide");
        }
        return valeur.strip();
    }
}

record Point(double x, double y) {
     // A static field is allowed, but not an instance field
    private static final Point ORIGINE = new Point(0, 0);

    public static Point origine() {
        return ORIGINE;
    }

    public double distance() {
        return Math.sqrt(x * x + y * y);
    }
}
    • Lines 30–36: the compact constructor. It is written without a parameter list; its parameters are implicitly those of the canonical constructor ([prenom], [nom], [age]). Its code executes first; then the fields are automatically initialized with the values—which may have been modified—of the parameters. Here, the first name and last name are validated and stripped of their leading and trailing spaces (lines 31–32), and a negative age is rejected (lines 33–35). In a compact constructor, you cannot assign values to fields ([this.prenom = ...] is rejected): you modify the parameters;
    • lines 39–41: a record may have other constructors, but these must call the canonical constructor with [this(...)]: any creation of [Personne] thus goes through the compact constructor’s validations;
    • lines 44–46: a record is immutable; aging it means creating a new instance;
    • lines 53–58: a static private validation method;
    • lines 61–72: A record can have static fields (line 63) and static methods (lines 65–67), such as the static factory [origine], but no instance fields in addition to its components.

    4.12. No extension methods: static utility methods

    How do you add a method to a class that cannot be modified, such as the [String] class derived from JDK? Some languages, such as C# or Kotlin, offer “extension methods”: static methods that are used like instance methods of the extended type. Java does not have them. Instead, we write static methods, grouped together in a utility class, and call them using the name of their class, passing the object as a parameter. The JDK program is full of them: [Arrays], [Collections], [Objects], [Math]… The program [Classes24.java] illustrates this:

    // No extension methods in Java: static utility methods
import static java.lang.Character.toUpperCase;

void main() {
    Personne p = new Personne("jean", "dupont", 30);
     // Utility methods are called using their class name
    IO.println(Outils.initiales(p));
    IO.println(Outils.premiereMajuscule("jean"));
    IO.println(Outils.nomComplet(p) + " est majeur : " + Outils.estMajeur(p));
    IO.println("\"il fait beau\" a " + Outils.nbMots("il fait beau") + " mots");
     // a static method of the record itself
    Personne inconnue = Personne.inconnue();
    IO.println(Outils.nomComplet(inconnue) + " est majeur : " + Outils.estMajeur(inconnue));
}

// a person
record Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age) {
     // static factory: an unknown person
    static Personne inconnue() {
        return new Personne("?", "?", 0);
    }
}

// a utility class: final, private constructor, static methods
final class Outils {
    private Outils() {
    }

    static String initiales(Personne p) {
        return toUpperCase(p.prenom().charAt(0)) + "." + toUpperCase(p.nom().charAt(0)) + ".";
    }

    static String premiereMajuscule(String s) {
        return s.isEmpty() ? s : toUpperCase(s.charAt(0)) + s.substring(1);
    }

    static boolean estMajeur(Personne p) {
        return p.age() >= 18;
    }

    static String nomComplet(Personne p) {
        return premiereMajuscule(p.prenom()) + " " + p.nom().toUpperCase();
    }

    static int nbMots(String s) {
        return s.isBlank() ? 0 : s.strip().split("\\s+").length;
    }
}
    • lines 25–48: the utility class [Outils]. It is final, and its sole constructor is private (lines 26–27): it cannot be derived from or instantiated. All of its methods are static;
    • lines 29–31: the method [initiales] takes the person as a parameter. Like a utility class written in another file, it uses only the public members of the person class—in this case, its accessors (in a compact file, however, it would have access to private fields); [charAt(0)] returns the first character of a string;
    • line 2: The static import of the method [Character.toUpperCase], which capitalizes a character, allows it to be called without its class name (lines 30 and 34);
    • lines 45–47: the method [nbMots] splits the string using the method [split], whose parameter is a regular expression: ["\\s+"] matches a sequence of one or more whitespace characters;
    • lines 7–10: Utility methods are called using the class name: [Outils.initiales(p)], not [p.initiales()];
    • lines 19–21: when the type can be modified, its methods are naturally placed there: the static factory [inconnue] is a method of the record [Personne] (line 12).

    // pattern matching on objects
void main() {
    Object[] objets = {
        new Particulier("Jean", "Dupont", 30),
        new Particulier("Lise", "Morel", 12),
        new Enseignant("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61),
        new Enseignant("Marc", "Petit", 44, 27),
        new Etudiant("Paul", "Martin", 19, "informatique"),
        "une chaîne",
        42,
        null,
    };

     // 1 - the type pattern: instanceof Type variable (Java 16)
    for (Object o : objets) {
        if (o instanceof Personne p) {
             // Here, p is a Person
            IO.println(p.prenom() + " est de type " + p.getClass().getSimpleName());
        }
    }

     // 2 - the type pattern followed by a condition
    for (Object o : objets) {
        if (o instanceof Personne p && p.age() >= 18) {
            IO.println(p.prenom() + " est majeur");
        }
    }

     // 3 - a switch statement on the object’s type, with guards and record patterns (Java 21)
    for (Object o : objets) {
        IO.println(decrire(o));
    }

     // 4 - an exhaustive switch on a sealed interface
    for (Object o : objets) {
        if (o instanceof Personne p) {
            IO.println(p.prenom() + " : " + categorie(p));
        }
    }
}

String decrire(Object o) {
    return switch (o) {
        case Enseignant e when e.section() == 27 -> e.prenom() + " enseigne l'informatique";
        case Enseignant e -> e.prenom() + " enseigne dans la section " + e.section();
        case Etudiant(var prenom, _, _, var filiere) -> prenom + " étudie " + filiere;
        case Personne p when p.age() < 18 -> p.prenom() + " est mineur";
        case Personne p -> p.prenom() + " a " + p.age() + " ans";
        case String s -> "une chaîne de " + s.length() + " caractères";
        case Integer n when n > 0 -> "l'entier positif " + n;
        case null -> "la référence null";
        default -> "un objet inconnu";
    };
}

// no default: the compiler knows that the three cases cover all people
String categorie(Personne p) {
    return switch (p) {
        case Particulier _ -> "particulier";
        case Enseignant _ -> "enseignant";
        case Etudiant _ -> "étudiant";
    };
}

// A sealed interface and the three records that implement it
sealed interface Personne permits Particulier, Enseignant, Etudiant {
    String prenom();
    String nom();
    int age();
}

record Particulier(String prenom, String nom, int age) implements Personne {
}

record Enseignant(String prenom, String nom, int age, int section) implements Personne {
}

record Etudiant(String prenom, String nom, int age, String filiere) implements Personne {
}
    • Lines 66–79: A sealed interface [Personne], implemented by three records: [Particulier], [Enseignant], and [Etudiant]. The interface declares the methods [prenom], [nom], and [age]: the records automatically implement them through their accessors, since they have components with the same names. Since a record is final, it can implement a sealed interface without further specification;
    • lines 3–12: an array of objects of various types, including an integer (automatically converted to *[Integer]) and the reference *[null];
    • line 16: the pattern of type [o instanceof Personne p] (Java 16) is true if [o] references an object of type [Personne]; in this case, the variable [p], of type [Personne], references this object. This avoids the sequence used in Java prior to version 16: testing the type with [instanceof], then converting with [(Personne) o]. The pattern is false if [o] is equal to [null];
    • line 24: the pattern variable [p] can be used in the rest of the condition, after [&&]: Java does not have property patterns; field values are tested using a condition;
    • lines 42–54: the expression [switch] on an object (Java 21) tries the patterns in order and returns the value associated with the first one that matches:
      • line 44: a teacher from section 27. The clause [when] adds a condition, called a guard, to the type pattern;
      • line 45: any other teacher. The order is important: if placed before the previous one, this pattern would have made it inaccessible, which the compiler would have reported as an error;
      • line 46: a record pattern: it extracts the components of the record [Etudiant] in the order they are declared; [var] lets the compiler infer their type, and the character [_] (Java 22) ignores a component;
      • lines 47–48: a minor, followed by any other person;
      • line 50: a positive integer;
      • line 51: the case [null]. Without it, a [switch] on a null reference throws a [NullPointerException] exception;
      • line 52: the case [default] handles everything else. Without it, the compiler would report that the expression [switch] does not cover all cases: a [switch] on an object must be exhaustive;
    • lines 57–63: a [switch] on a [Personne], without [default]. However, it is exhaustive: since the interface is sealed, the compiler knows that a person is either a [Particulier], a [Enseignant], or a [Etudiant]. The pattern [Particulier _] tests the type without declaring a variable.

    This is the great advantage of combining sealed types with pattern filtering: if a fourth record is added to the hierarchy, the compiler identifies all the [switch] records that need to be filled in. Note also that the type pattern corresponds to the types that implement the interface: the type pattern loop (lines 15–20) has selected the three types of people. Pattern filtering is a useful alternative to cascading [if (o instanceof ...)] statements; however, it should not replace polymorphism: when behavior depends on the object’s type and the class hierarchy is well-defined, a method redefined in each class often remains the object-oriented solution. Pattern-based filtering is well-suited for data hierarchies (records) on which one wishes to write processing logic external to that data.

    4.14. Handling the null value

    Any reference-type variable can have the value [null], and using a null reference causes the [NullPointerException] exception, the most common runtime error in Java. Unlike other languages such as C# or Kotlin, the Java compiler does not distinguish between types that can be [null] and those that cannot. However, the JDK and libraries provide several tools to mitigate this risk:

    • the [Optional<T>] class (Java 8), the return type of a method that may return nothing;
    • the methods of the [Objects] class: [requireNonNull] to reject [null] at the entry point of a method or constructor, and [requireNonNullElse] to provide a default value;
    • annotations that document intent and are verified by certain analysis tools. The most recent ones, proposed by a group of vendors (Google, JetBrains, Spring…), are those from the JSpecify library: [@Nullable] on a type that can be [null], and [@NullMarked] on a class or package to indicate that other types cannot be. Spring Framework 7, which we will be using, employs them. They require a library, so we will not use them in this chapter.

    // Handling the null value: Optional, Objects.requireNonNull...
void main() {
    Personne jean = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont");
    jean.setSecondPrenom("Marie");
    Personne[] personnes = { jean, new Personne("Paul", "Martin") };
    for (Personne p : personnes) {
         // a default value when the reference is null
        String second = Objects.requireNonNullElse(p.getSecondPrenom(), "(aucun)");
         // an explicit check
        String longueur = p.getSecondPrenom() == null ? "null" : String.valueOf(p.getSecondPrenom().length());
        IO.println(p.getPrenom() + " : second prénom=" + second + ", longueur=" + longueur);
    }

     // a method that may return nothing: it returns an Optional<Person>
    Optional<Personne> trouvee = chercher(personnes, "Durand");
    IO.println("Durand trouvé : " + trouvee.isPresent());
    IO.println(trouvee.map(Personne::getPrenom).orElse("Durand : personne non trouvée"));
     // we check for the presence of a value before using it
    trouvee = chercher(personnes, "Martin");
    if (trouvee.isPresent()) {
        IO.println("Martin : " + trouvee.get().getPrenom());
    }
     // ifPresent: the action is performed only if a value is present
    chercher(personnes, "Dupont").ifPresent(p -> p.setSecondPrenom("Louise"));
    chercher(personnes, "Durand").ifPresent(p -> p.setSecondPrenom("Louise"));
    IO.println(jean.getSecondPrenom());
     // orElseThrow: we assert that the value is present; otherwise, an exception is thrown
    Personne martin = chercher(personnes, "Martin").orElseThrow();
    IO.println(martin.getPrenom());

     // Objects.requireNonNull: a required parameter
    try {
        new Personne(null, "Morel");
    } catch (NullPointerException ex) {
        IO.println("Erreur : " + ex.getMessage());
    }
     // the exception NullPointerException and its detailed message (Java 14)
    try {
        Personne lise = new Personne("Lise", "Morel");
        IO.println(lise.getSecondPrenom().length());
    } catch (NullPointerException ex) {
        IO.println("Erreur : " + ex.getMessage());
    }
}

// Searching for a person by name
Optional<Personne> chercher(Personne[] personnes, String nom) {
    for (Personne p : personnes) {
        if (p.getNom().equals(nom)) {
            return Optional.of(p);
        }
    }
    return Optional.empty();
}

class Personne {
     // Required fields: they must never be null
    private final String prenom;
    private final String nom;
     // Optional field: `null` means “no middle name”
    private String secondPrenom;

    public Personne(String prenom, String nom) {
        this.prenom = Objects.requireNonNull(prenom, "le prénom est obligatoire");
        this.nom = Objects.requireNonNull(nom, "le nom est obligatoire");
    }

    public String getPrenom() {
        return prenom;
    }

    public String getNom() {
        return nom;
    }

    public String getSecondPrenom() {
        return secondPrenom;
    }

    public void setSecondPrenom(String secondPrenom) {
        this.secondPrenom = secondPrenom;
    }
}
    • lines 56–83: The [Personne] class has two required fields, initialized by the constructor, and one optional field, [secondPrenom]: [null] means “no middle name.” The constructor rejects a first name or last name of [null] when paired with [Objects.requireNonNull] (lines 64–65): the error is detected when the object is created rather than much later, when the field is used;
    • line 8: [Objects.requireNonNullElse(valeur, défaut)] (Java 9) returns [valeur] if it is not equal to [null]; otherwise, it returns [défaut];
    • line 10: An explicit check is often the simplest approach;
    • lines 47–54: The method [chercher] returns the person being searched for wrapped in a [Optional] object, or an empty [Optional]: its return type, [Optional<Personne>], warns the caller that the result may be missing, and requires the caller to handle this case to retrieve the person. [Optional.of(p)] creates a [Optional] containing [p], [Optional.empty()], and an empty [Optional];
    • line 16: [isPresent] indicates whether [Optional] contains a value;
    • line 17: [map(Personne::getPrenom)] converts any person present into their first name; [orElse(valeur)] returns the present value or, if none, the specified value. The notation [Personne::getPrenom] is a method reference, which we will examine in Chapter 7; here, it refers to “the person’s [getPrenom] method”;
    • lines 20–22: [get] returns the present value; it is called only after verifying its presence;
    • lines 24–25: [ifPresent] executes the specified action only if a value is present. The action is a lambda (Chapter 7): [p -> p.setSecondPrenom("Louise")] reads “for person p, set their middle name.” Dupont exists and is assigned a new middle name; Durand does not exist, and the statement does nothing;
    • Line 28: [orElseThrow] returns the value if it is present, or throws a [NoSuchElementException] exception if [Optional] is empty. This is used when you are certain the value is present;
    • lines 32–36: A person without a first name is rejected by the constructor;
    • lines 38–43: Using a null reference throws the [NullPointerException] exception. Since Java 14, its message specifically identifies the null expression.

    [Optional] is intended for method return values; it is not used for fields or parameters. In this course, we document whether a value is optional, verify required parameters using [Objects.requireNonNull], and prefer objects that are always complete (constructed with all their required values) over objects that are populated incrementally.

    4.15. Example Application - V2

    We’ll revisit the tax calculation already covered in the previous chapter (version 1) and now implement it using classes and interfaces. Let’s review the problem. We aim to write a program to calculate a taxpayer’s tax. We’ll consider the simplified case of a taxpayer who has only their salary to report (the 2004 tax schedule for 2003 income, used as-is: this is an exercise):

    • we calculate the employee’s number of tax brackets: nbParts = nbEnfants / 2 + 1 if they are unmarried, nbEnfants / 2 + 2 if he is married, where nbEnfants is the number of his children;
    • if he has at least three children, he receives an additional half-share;
    • his taxable income R is calculated as R = 0.72 × S, where S is his annual salary;
    • his family quotient is calculated as QF = R / nbParts;
    • his tax I is calculated using the following table:
    threshold
    coeffR
    coeffN
    4962
    0
    0
    8382
    0.068
    291.09
    14,753
    0.191
    1,322.92
    23,888
    0.283
    2,668.39
    38,868
    0.374
    4,846.98
    47,932
    0.426
    6,883.66
    0
    0.481
    9,505.54

    Each row has three fields. To calculate tax I, find the first row where QF ≤ the limit. For example, if QF = 5,000, the row (8,382; 0.068; 291.09) will be found. Tax I is then equal to 0.068 × R - 291.09 × nbParts. If QF is such that the condition QF ≤ limit is never satisfied, then the coefficients of the last row are used, resulting in tax I = 0.481 × R - 9,505.54 × nbParts.

    The application generates the file [ImpotsV2]. The calculation classes are organized into a package named [impots]:

    1

    First, we define a type capable of encapsulating a row from the previous array [TrancheImpot.java]:

    1
2
3
4
5
6
7
    package impots;

import java.math.BigDecimal;

// a tax bracket
public record TrancheImpot(BigDecimal limite, BigDecimal coeffR, BigDecimal coeffN) {
}

    We use a record:

    • because a slice is a small piece of data without an identity, defined solely by its value, and there is no reason for it to be modified once created: a record is immutable;
    • because the compiler generates the constructor, the accessors, [toString], and the equality operator from a single line.

    The components are of type [BigDecimal] (package [java.math], hence the import on line 3). The types [float] and [double] represent numbers in binary: a decimal number such as 0.068 has no exact representation in them, and calculations accumulate small rounding errors. The [BigDecimal] class represents decimal numbers exactly: this is the type to use for amounts. Its drawback is the lack of operators: we write [a.add(b)], [a.multiply(b)], [a.compareTo(b)].

    Next, we define an interface [IImpot] capable of calculating the tax [IImpot.java]:

    1
2
3
4

    package impots;

public interface IImpot {
     // Calculation of a taxpayer’s tax
    int calculer(boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire);
}
    • Line 5: The method for calculating the tax based on three pieces of data: the taxpayer’s marital status, the number of children, and annual salary. It rounds the tax down to the nearest euro.
