    package impots;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.MathContext;
import java.util.List;

public abstract class AbstractImpot implements IImpot {
     // The tax brackets required for the calculation come from an external source
     // known only to derived classes
    protected abstract List<TrancheImpot> getTranchesImpot();

     // tax calculation
    @Override
    public int calculer(boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire) {
         // Calculation of the number of shares
        BigDecimal nbParts = BigDecimal.valueOf(nbEnfants).divide(BigDecimal.TWO)
                .add(BigDecimal.valueOf(marie ? 2 : 1));
        if (nbEnfants >= 3) {
            nbParts = nbParts.add(new BigDecimal("0.5"));
        }
         // Calculation of taxable income and the family quotient
        BigDecimal revenu = new BigDecimal("0.72").multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(salaire));
        BigDecimal quotient = revenu.divide(nbParts, MathContext.DECIMAL128);
         // Determination of the tax bracket: the last one is used if no other limit applies
        List<TrancheImpot> tranches = getTranchesImpot();
        TrancheImpot tranche = tranches.getLast();
        for (int i = 0; i < tranches.size() - 1; i++) {
            if (quotient.compareTo(tranches.get(i).limite()) <= 0) {
                tranche = tranches.get(i);
                break;
            }
        }
         // tax calculation
        return revenu.multiply(tranche.coeffR()).subtract(nbParts.multiply(tranche.coeffN())).intValue();
    }
}
    • Line 1: The class belongs to the [impots] package; its file is therefore in the [impots] folder;
    • Line 7: The class [AbstractImpot] implements the interface [IImpot];
    • Line 10: The scale data, provided by a protected abstract method. The [AbstractImpot] class does not know where this data comes from (written in the code, read from a file, a database, etc.). It leaves this up to the derived classes. This is why it is declared abstract, which prevents it from being instantiated. The abstract method requires derived classes to provide the brackets; the compiler verifies this;
    • lines 13–35: the implementation of the [calculer] method of the [IImpot] interface. Derived classes will not need to rewrite this method. The [AbstractImpot] class thus serves as a factorization class for the derived classes: it contains what is common to all of them;
    • lines 16–17: the number of shares. [BigDecimal.valueOf(n)] converts an integer to [BigDecimal]; division by [BigDecimal.TWO] is exact (3 / 2 = 1.5), unlike integer division by [nbEnfants / 2] (3 / 2 = 1). The expression [marie ? 2 : 1] equals 2 for a married taxpayer, 1 otherwise;
    • lines 18–20: the additional half-share. A [BigDecimal] is immutable: [add] returns a new object, which must be assigned to the variable;
    • lines 22–23: taxable income and the family quotient. Decimal constants are created from strings ([new BigDecimal("0.72")]) to ensure they are exact. Dividing a [BigDecimal] can result in an infinite number of decimal places (1 / 3): we specify the desired precision, in this case [MathContext.DECIMAL128] (34 significant digits);
    • lines 25–32: searching for the bracket. By default, this is the last bracket ([tranches.getLast()], line 26). The loop iterates through all brackets except the last one and stops ([break]) at the first bracket whose limit is greater than or equal to the family quotient, as tested by [compareTo(...) <= 0];
    • line 34: the tax calculation. The method [intValue] truncates the result to its integer part.

    A class that implements the [IImpot] interface can be created by deriving it from the [AbstractImpot] class. This is what we are now doing with [HardwiredImpot.java]:

    package impots;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class HardwiredImpot extends AbstractImpot {
     // tax calculation data (2004 tax schedule for 2003 income), hard-coded
    private static final double[] LIMITES = { 4962, 8382, 14753, 23888, 38868, 47932, 0 };
    private static final double[] COEFF_R = { 0, 0.068, 0.191, 0.283, 0.374, 0.426, 0.481 };
    private static final double[] COEFF_N = { 0, 291.09, 1322.92, 2668.39, 4846.98, 6883.66, 9505.54 };

     // Tax brackets
    private final List<TrancheImpot> tranchesImpot;

     // program generator
    public HardwiredImpot() {
         // Creation and population of the tax bracket list
        List<TrancheImpot> tranches = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < LIMITES.length; i++) {
            tranches.add(new TrancheImpot(BigDecimal.valueOf(LIMITES[i]),
                    BigDecimal.valueOf(COEFF_R[i]), BigDecimal.valueOf(COEFF_N[i])));
        }
         // The stored list cannot be modified
        tranchesImpot = List.copyOf(tranches);
    }

     // Implementation of the parent class's abstract method
    @Override
    protected List<TrancheImpot> getTranchesImpot() {
        return tranchesImpot;
    }
}
    • Lines 9–11: The class [HardwiredImpot] hardcodes the data needed to calculate the tax. These are class fields ([static]) [final]: they are shared by all instances and cannot be replaced by other arrays. By convention, the names of the constants ([static final]) are written in uppercase;
    • lines 17–26: the constructor uses this data to build the list of tax brackets. [BigDecimal.valueOf(double)] (lines 21–22) converts a [double] to a [BigDecimal] via its shortest decimal representation: [BigDecimal.valueOf(0.068)] is exactly 0.068. Do not use the constructor [new BigDecimal(0.068)], which reproduces all the decimal places of the approximated binary value (0.068000000000000004884981308350688…);
    • line 25: [List.copyOf] returns a read-only copy of the list: no class will be able to modify the scale;
    • lines 29–32: the parent class’s abstract method is implemented: it returns the list of brackets.

    The next chapter will add other classes derived from [AbstractImpot], which will read the brackets from a text file or from JSON: they will only need to provide the [getTranchesImpot] method.

    // Interactive tax calculation program
// The user enters three pieces of data via the keyboard: married nbEnfants salary
// The program then displays the tax due
import impots.HardwiredImpot;
import impots.IImpot;

static final String SYNTAXE = """
        syntaxe : Marié NbEnfants Salaire
        Marié : o pour marié, n pour non marié
        NbEnfants : nombre d'enfants
        Salaire : salaire annuel en euros""";

void main() {
     // creation of an object IImpot
    IImpot impot = new HardwiredImpot();

     // input loop
    while (true) {
         // The program prompts for the tax calculation parameters
        String parametres = IO.readln("Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : "
                + "Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : ");
         // End of standard input or empty line: the program stops
        if (parametres == null || parametres.isBlank()) {
            break;
        }
         // Check the number of fields in the entered line
        String[] champs = parametres.strip().split("\\s+");
        if (champs.length != 3) {
            IO.println(SYNTAXE);
            continue;
        }
         // Checking the validity of the parameters
         // married
        String marie = champs[0].toLowerCase();
        if (!marie.equals("o") && !marie.equals("n")) {
            IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument marié incorrect : tapez o ou n");
            continue;
        }
         // nbEnfants
        int nbEnfants = entierPositif(champs[1]);
        if (nbEnfants < 0) {
            IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument NbEnfants incorrect : tapez un entier positif ou nul");
            continue;
        }
         // salary
        int salaire = entierPositif(champs[2]);
        if (salaire < 0) {
            IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument salaire incorrect : tapez un entier positif ou nul");
            continue;
        }
         // Parameters are correct: calculate tax
        IO.println("Impôt=" + impot.calculer(marie.equals("o"), nbEnfants, salaire) + " euros");
    }
}

// returns the positive integer or zero represented by the string; returns -1 if the string does not represent one
int entierPositif(String chaine) {
    try {
        int valeur = Integer.parseInt(chaine);
        return valeur >= 0 ? valeur : -1;
    } catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
        return -1;
    }
}

    The program above allows the user to perform repeated tax calculation simulations.

    • Lines 4–5: The main program is in the unnamed package; it imports the two types it needs from the [impots] package. These types must be public;
    • Lines 7–11: The help message is a constant of the implicit class, written as a text block (Java 15) delimited by three quotation marks: the string can span multiple lines, and the common indentation of the lines is removed. Since the closing quotation mark is placed at the end of the last line, the string does not end with a line break;
    • line 15: creation of a [impot] object that implements the [IImpot] interface. This object is obtained by instantiating a type [HardwiredImpot], a type that implements the interface [IImpot]. Note that the variable [impot] was not assigned the type [HardwiredImpot] but rather the type [IImpot]. By writing this, we indicate that we are only interested in the [calculer] method of the [impot] object and not in the rest. To use data from a file, simply change this single line;
    • lines 18–53: the loop for tax calculation simulations;
    • lines 20–21: the three parameters required for the [calculer] method are requested in a single line entered via the keyboard. [IO.readln(message)] displays the message and then reads a line; it returns [null] if standard input is closed: the check on line 23 then terminates the program, just as an empty line would;
    • line 27: the [split] method splits the line—with leading and trailing spaces removed—into words separated by one or more space characters (regular expression ["\\s+"]);
    • Lines 40 and 46: The method [entierPositif] (lines 57–64) verifies that the last two fields are positive integers or zero. [Integer.parseInt] throws a [NumberFormatException] exception if the string does not represent an integer: the method catches it and returns -1, which indicates an error;
    • line 52: call to the [calculer] method of the [impot] object implementing the [IImpot] interface.

    The tax amounts are calculated correctly: 4,282 euros for a married taxpayer with two children and an annual salary of 60,000 euros (line 26), and 2,959 euros with three children (line 28). An unmarried taxpayer with no children pays 11,519 euros for the same salary (line 30).

    Compared to Version 1, the calculation is now encapsulated in classes behind an interface: the dialog program only recognizes the [IImpot] interface. Subsequent versions will take advantage of this separation: Version 3 (next chapter) will change the data source by deriving new classes from [AbstractImpot], and then the application will be organized into layers (Chapter 6).
